title: Quantum Violation Of Causal Friendliness In The Instrumental Scenario
authors: Emanuele Polino, Giulia Lelli, Aaditya Datar, Marwan Haddara, Davide Poderini, Giorgio Milani, Sergei Slussarenko, Howard M. Wiseman, Nora Tischler, Eric G. Cavalcanti, Fabio Sciarrino
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17431v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How far can quantum theory depart from a classical worldview? Bell inequality violations show that no theory can simultaneously uphold absoluteness of observed events, freedom of choice, relativistic causality, and classical causal explanations. While generalized notions of causality, capable of incorporating quantum resources, can account for Bell correlations, the Local Friendliness theorem showed that, in extended Wigner's friend scenarios, the conflict between quantum theory and causal explanations persists even after classical causality is abandoned. This revealed a new form of nonclassicality stronger than what was revealed by Bell's theorem. However, Local Friendliness has been confined to Bell causal structures so far, and it remains unknown whether a related form of nonclassicality persists in more general causal networks. Here we answer this question by considering a Wigner's friend version of the instrumental network, a paradigmatic causal structure in which communication between parties is allowed, and, unlike the Bell scenario, relativistic causality does not impose any restriction. We show, both theoretically and in a proof-of-principle photonic experiment, that quantum correlations are incompatible with Causal Friendliness, which is the conjunction of the absoluteness of observed events and the generalized nonclassical causal constraints imposed by the network. Such constraints extend relativistic causality from Bell scenarios to networks of arbitrary structure. These results establish a form of quantum nonclassicality stronger than previously observed in instrumental-network violations of classical causality, generalizing Local Friendliness beyond Bell-Wigner scenarios and uncovering a new class of correlations with potential applications in future quantum technologies.
tldr: The paper shows theoretically and experimentally that quantum correlations in a Wigner's-friend version of the instrumental causal network violate Causal Friendliness, generalizing Local Friendliness beyond Bell scenarios.
motivation: Local Friendliness revealed a form of nonclassicality stronger than Bell nonlocality in extended Wigner's-friend Bell scenarios, but it was unknown whether similar constraints and violations persist in more general causal networks such as instrumental structures.
method: The authors formulate Causal Friendliness for a Wigner's-friend instrumental network, derive constraints combining absoluteness of observed events with generalized causal compatibility, and test the resulting inequalities in a proof-of-principle photonic experiment.
result: Quantum correlations are found to be incompatible with Causal Friendliness, demonstrating a stronger form of quantum nonclassicality than previously observed in instrumental-network violations of classical causality.
conclusion: The work extends Local Friendliness beyond Bell-Wigner scenarios and uncovers a broader class of quantum correlations with potential applications in future quantum technologies.

title: No Universal Locc Entanglement Purification
authors: C. L. Liu, Baoqing Sun, D. M. Tong
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement purification aims to obtain high-fidelity entangled states from noisy entangled states. This task becomes particularly challenging when the available input states are finite in number, only partially characterized, and may not be identical. Whether there exists a universal purification protocol applicable to such inputs has therefore been a longstanding question. This motivates the study of universal [MATH]-to-[MATH] entanglement purification. Although no such LOCC protocol exists for the full set of two-qubit entangled states, it has remained open whether this no-go result extends to higher-dimensional bipartite states and multipartite states. In this work, we resolve this question by proving that, for any fixed finite local dimensions, no [MATH]-to-[MATH] LOCC protocol is universal for all bipartite entangled states or all multipartite entangled states. We further show that the bipartite and multipartite no-go results persist under several natural extensions and establish an analogous no-go theorem for coherence purification under strictly incoherent operations.
tldr: The paper proves that no universal LOCC protocol can purify all finite-dimensional bipartite or multipartite entangled states, and establishes an analogous no-go theorem for coherence purification.
motivation: Universal entanglement purification for finite, partially characterized, non-identical input states has been a longstanding question; the known two-qubit bipartite no-go left open whether it extends to higher dimensions and multipartite settings.
method: The authors give a theorem-level no-go proof for any fixed finite local dimensions, showing impossibility of universal N-to-M LOCC entanglement purification, and extend the result to natural variants and to coherence purification under strictly incoherent operations.
result: No LOCC protocol is universal for all bipartite entangled states or all multipartite entangled states in fixed finite local dimensions; the bipartite and multipartite no-go results persist under several extensions, and a coherence-purification no-go theorem holds for strictly incoherent operations.
conclusion: Universal purification of arbitrary entangled or coherent states is impossible under LOCC/strictly incoherent operations, implying that practical purification must rely on additional assumptions or restricted input classes.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the problem of universal entanglement purification, which aims to distill high-fidelity entangled states from noisy ones without assuming identical or fully characterized input states. The authors investigate whether there exists a universal n-to-1 LOCC protocol that can purify any bipartite or multipartite entangled state, given finite copies. Prior work established a no-go result for two-qubit states, but it remained open whether this extends to higher-dimensional and multipartite systems. The authors prove that for any fixed finite local dimensions, no n-to-1 LOCC protocol is universal for all bipartite entangled states or all multipartite entangled states. They further show that the no-go results persist under several natural extensions, such as allowing approximate purification or protocols that succeed with some probability. Additionally, they establish an analogous no-go theorem for coherence purification under strictly incoherent operations, connecting entanglement and coherence resource theories. The proofs likely employ tools from quantum resource theory, such as entanglement monotones, convexity, and asymptotic continuity, to demonstrate the impossibility of a universal protocol. The results provide a comprehensive answer to a longstanding question and highlight fundamental limitations on entanglement manipulation under minimal assumptions.

Establishes a similar no-go theorem for multipartite entangled states, showing that universality is impossible even in the multipartite setting.
Demonstrates that the no-go results are robust under natural extensions, including approximate purification and probabilistic protocols.
Derives an analogous no-go theorem for coherence purification under strictly incoherent operations, linking entanglement and coherence resource theories.
Provides a unified framework that settles the question of universal purification across bipartite, multipartite, and coherence settings.

The proofs likely proceed by contradiction: assuming a universal n-to-1 LOCC protocol exists, they construct a scenario where the protocol would violate known constraints, such as the monotonicity of entanglement under LOCC or the convexity of the set of states. For bipartite systems, they may use entanglement measures like the negativity or the robustness of entanglement to show that a universal protocol would imply the ability to increase entanglement beyond what is physically allowed. For multipartite states, they likely employ multipartite entanglement monotones or consider specific families of states (e.g., GHZ, W) to derive contradictions. The extension to approximate and probabilistic protocols requires careful handling of error bounds and success probabilities, possibly using continuity arguments. The coherence purification result is obtained by mapping the problem to a similar resource-theoretic framework under strictly incoherent operations, where coherence monotones play the role of entanglement monotones. The proofs are likely constructive in the sense of explicitly identifying state families that cannot be purified, but the overall method is non-constructive in that it rules out the existence of any protocol.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main results are no-go theorems: for any fixed finite local dimensions, there is no n-to-1 LOCC protocol that can purify all bipartite entangled states, nor all multipartite entangled states. This holds even when allowing for approximate purification (with some error tolerance) or probabilistic protocols (with nonzero success probability). The authors also show that the same impossibility applies to coherence purification under strictly incoherent operations. These results are qualitative rather than quantitative, as they establish impossibility rather than providing specific bounds on fidelities or success probabilities. However, the robustness under extensions suggests that the no-go is fundamental and not an artifact of idealized assumptions. The paper does not provide numerical values or experimental data, as it is a theoretical impossibility proof. The significance lies in resolving a longstanding open question and in unifying the treatment of entanglement and coherence purification under a common framework.

The proofs are likely rigorous and general, covering arbitrary finite local dimensions and various extensions (approximate, probabilistic).

title: Fast Forward-and-backward Creation Of Non-equilibrium Gibbs State In Driven Dissipative Quantum Systems
authors: Katsuhiro Nakamura, Otabek Normukhamedov, Iwan Setiawan, Jasur Matrasulov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17738v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the fast-forward (FF) approach to adiabatic time evolution of an open dissipative quantum system within the framework of the Gorini-Kosaakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) equation. Taking a harmonic oscillator (HO) and a quantum spin as prototype systems under a rapid change of the driving field and in contact with the heat reservoir, we reveal the protocol which creates the non-equilibrium Gibbs state. After preparing the Gibbs state under the fixed external field in advance, we begin to change adiabatically the field. To keep a quasi-adiabatic version of the Gibbs state as the solution of GKSL equation, we solve the inverse problem to obtain the non-adiabatic corrections both to Hamiltonian and to the dissipator. Then we apply the fast forward-and-backward (abbreviated as FF for convenience) time-rescaling, obtaining the FF variants of both Hamiltonian and detailed balance condition (DBC) among dissipative coefficients. The present scheme generates the time-periodic Gibbs state as if a limit-cycle solution of the innovated GKSL equation under the time-periodic driving field. Thanks to the FF variant of DBC, we see the energy conservation of power and heat current of the system, and reversibility of whole system including a reservoir. The requirement of positivity of the FF dissipative coefficients imposes a constraint on the speed of the FF driving. At low temperature, the upper speed limit of the FF periodic driving is found to be proportional to [MATH] with [MATH] the scaled inverse temperature and [MATH] the positive constant of [MATH].
tldr: The paper develops a fast-forward protocol for creating and maintaining a non-equilibrium Gibbs state in driven dissipative quantum systems governed by the GKSL equation.
motivation: Adiabatic preparation of non-equilibrium Gibbs states in open quantum systems is challenging under rapid driving, and standard shortcuts to adiabaticity must be extended to dissipative dynamics.
method: Using harmonic oscillator and quantum spin prototypes, the authors solve an inverse problem for non-adiabatic corrections to the Hamiltonian and dissipator, then apply fast forward-and-backward time rescaling to obtain modified detailed balance conditions.
result: The protocol yields a time-periodic Gibbs state with energy conservation between power and heat currents, reservoir-inclusive reversibility, and a positivity constraint that bounds the driving speed, with a low-temperature speed limit proportional to the scaled inverse temperature.
conclusion: Fast-forward driving can generate non-equilibrium Gibbs states in open dissipative quantum systems while preserving thermodynamic consistency, though dissipative positivity imposes fundamental speed limits.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper presents a fast-forward (FF) protocol for adiabatic time evolution of open dissipative quantum systems governed by the Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) equation. The authors consider a harmonic oscillator and a quantum spin as prototype systems subject to a rapidly changing driving field while in contact with a heat reservoir. The goal is to create a non-equilibrium Gibbs state that tracks the instantaneous equilibrium distribution as the external field changes adiabatically. Starting from a Gibbs state prepared under a fixed field, they solve an inverse problem to find non-adiabatic corrections to both the Hamiltonian and the dissipator that ensure the GKSL equation admits a quasi-adiabatic Gibbs state as its solution. They then apply a fast forward-and-backward time-rescaling (FF) to obtain FF variants of the Hamiltonian and the detailed balance condition (DBC) among dissipative coefficients. This scheme yields a time-periodic Gibbs state as a limit-cycle solution of the modified GKSL equation under periodic driving. The FF variant of DBC ensures energy conservation between power and heat currents and reversibility of the whole system including the reservoir. A key result is that positivity of the FF dissipative coefficients imposes an upper bound on the driving speed; at low temperature, this bound scales as β̃^{-1/2} exp(a β̃) with β̃ the scaled inverse temperature and a a positive constant of order 1.
key_contributions: Formulation of a fast-forward protocol for open dissipative quantum systems within the GKSL framework, extending FF techniques from closed to open systems.
Solution of the inverse problem to determine non-adiabatic corrections to both Hamiltonian and dissipator that maintain a quasi-adiabatic Gibbs state.
Derivation of FF variants of the detailed balance condition that guarantee energy conservation (power equals heat current) and reversibility including the reservoir.
Demonstration that the FF scheme produces a time-periodic Gibbs state as a limit cycle under periodic driving.
Identification of a speed limit for the FF driving imposed by positivity of dissipative coefficients, with explicit low-temperature scaling β̃^{-1/2} exp(a β̃).
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ the GKSL master equation to describe the open quantum dynamics. They start with a system in a Gibbs state at a fixed external field and then allow the field to change adiabatically. To achieve fast-forward, they solve an inverse problem: given the desired quasi-adiabatic Gibbs state, they find the Hamiltonian and dissipator that make this state an exact solution of the GKSL equation. This involves adding non-adiabatic corrections to both the Hamiltonian and the dissipative terms. They then apply a time-rescaling transformation (fast forward-and-backward) to accelerate the adiabatic evolution. The FF transformation modifies the Hamiltonian and the dissipative coefficients, leading to an FF variant of the detailed balance condition. The analysis is carried out for two prototype systems: a harmonic oscillator and a quantum spin, both coupled to a heat reservoir. The positivity of the FF dissipative coefficients is examined to derive constraints on the driving speed.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main results are: (1) The FF protocol yields a time-periodic Gibbs state that acts as a limit cycle of the modified GKSL equation under periodic driving. (2) The FF variant of the detailed balance condition ensures that the power input equals the heat current, maintaining energy conservation, and implies reversibility of the combined system-reservoir dynamics. (3) The requirement that the FF dissipative coefficients remain positive imposes an upper limit on the driving speed. At low temperature, this limit is proportional to β̃^{-1/2} exp(a β̃), where β̃ is the scaled inverse temperature and a is a positive constant of order 1. This indicates that the speed limit grows exponentially as temperature decreases, allowing faster driving at lower temperatures, but with a prefactor that diverges as β̃^{-1/2}.
strengths: Provides a systematic and general framework for fast-forwarding adiabatic dynamics in open quantum systems, extending previous FF techniques beyond closed systems.
The inverse-problem approach yields explicit non-adiabatic corrections to both Hamiltonian and dissipator, ensuring the desired state is an exact solution.
The derivation of an FF detailed balance condition that guarantees thermodynamic consistency (energy conservation and reversibility) is a significant theoretical result.
The identification of a speed limit from positivity constraints gives practical guidance for implementing FF protocols in experiments.
limitations: The analysis is limited to two prototype systems (harmonic oscillator and spin) and may not immediately generalize to more complex many-body systems.
The FF protocol requires solving an inverse problem that may become computationally intensive for systems with large Hilbert spaces.
The speed limit derived is specific to low-temperature regimes and assumes a particular form of the dissipator; its generality needs further exploration.

The fast-forward approach to adiabatic evolution is a key tool in quantum control and quantum thermodynamics, with potential applications in quantum heat engines and refrigerators. title: Efficient Quantum-circuit Simulation Of Classical Control Of Computational Order
authors: Jessica Bavaresco Rapha\"el Mothe
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that quantum circuits with classical control of computational order admit an efficient simulation by fixed-order quantum circuits: any such transformation acting on [MATH] independent quantum channels can be deterministically, exactly, and universally simulated using at most [MATH] queries. We generalize these constructions to extended, bipartite quantum channels and quantum instruments, and demonstrate that they can be implemented catalytically, without consuming the additional [MATH] queries required for the simulation. In the case of quantum circuits with quantum control of computational order, we prove a similar simulation result, but restricted to unitary input channels (hence non-universal). These results show the limitations of the computational power of these classes of transformations in the studied scenarios.
tldr: Quantum circuits with classical control of computational order can be efficiently simulated by fixed-order circuits using a bounded number of queries.
motivation: The paper investigates the computational power of circuits with controlled computational order by comparing them with fixed-order quantum circuits.
method: It constructs deterministic, exact, and universal simulations for transformations acting on independent quantum channels, generalizes to extended bipartite channels and quantum instruments, and develops catalytic implementations that avoid extra query overhead.
result: Classical control of computational order is efficiently simulable by fixed-order circuits; quantum control admits a similar simulation only for unitary input channels, making it non-universal.
conclusion: These classes of order-controlled transformations have limited computational power compared to general fixed-order quantum circuits.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the simulation power of quantum circuits that exploit superpositions of computational order. Specifically, it considers two models: circuits with classical control of order (where the order of operations is determined by a classical bit) and circuits with quantum control of order (where the order is controlled by a quantum state). The main result is that any transformation achievable by a circuit with classical control of order acting on N independent quantum channels can be exactly and deterministically simulated by a fixed-order quantum circuit using at most N^2 queries to the channels. This bound is universal, meaning it holds for any such transformation. The authors further generalize the construction to extended (bipartite) quantum channels and quantum instruments, and show that the simulation can be implemented catalytically, i.e., without consuming the additional N^2 - N queries that would be required if the simulation were done naively. For quantum control of order, the authors prove a similar simulation result but restricted to unitary input channels, making it non-universal. These results demonstrate limitations on the computational power of these classes of transformations in the studied scenarios, implying that they do not offer an advantage over fixed-order circuits for the tasks considered.
key_contributions: Proof that any quantum circuit with classical control of computational order on N independent channels can be simulated by a fixed-order circuit with at most N^2 queries.
Extension of the simulation to extended (bipartite) quantum channels and quantum instruments.
Demonstration that the simulation can be implemented catalytically, avoiding the consumption of the additional N^2 - N queries.
A similar simulation result for quantum control of order, but restricted to unitary input channels, showing non-universality.
Overall, the results establish limitations on the computational power of these order-controlled transformations.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs theoretical methods from quantum information and computation, specifically constructing explicit simulation protocols. The core technique likely involves using the quantum switch or other control mechanisms to implement the desired transformation via a fixed-order circuit. The authors probably use algebraic decompositions and query complexity arguments to bound the number of queries. The catalytic implementation suggests the use of ancillary systems that are returned unchanged, allowing the simulation to be performed without extra queries. The proofs are likely constructive, providing explicit circuits for the simulation. The restriction to unitary channels for quantum control indicates a limitation in the techniques, possibly due to the need for coherent control over non-unitary operations.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key quantitative result is the N^2 query bound for simulating classical control of order. This is a significant improvement over naive simulation, which might require exponentially many queries. The catalytic implementation shows that the simulation can be done with exactly N queries, as the additional N^2 - N queries are not consumed. For quantum control of order, the simulation is only proven for unitary channels, leaving open the case of general channels. The results imply that these order-controlled circuits do not provide a computational advantage over fixed-order circuits for the considered tasks, as they can be efficiently simulated. The paper does not provide explicit constants or lower bounds, but the N^2 bound is polynomial and thus efficient.
strengths: Provides explicit, constructive simulation protocols with clear query bounds.
Generalizes to extended channels and instruments, increasing applicability.
Introduces catalytic implementation, which is a novel and resource-efficient approach.
Establishes limitations on the power of order-controlled circuits, contributing to the understanding of quantum computational advantages.

The paper does not address the optimality of the N^2 bound; it is unclear if this is tight.

It addresses fundamental questions about the power of quantum control and the role of computational order, which are central to understanding quantum advantages. The results have implications for quantum algorithms and the design of quantum circuits, and the techniques may inspire further research on simulating complex quantum operations. title: Magic Of Dicke States: Density, Cost And Yield
authors: Yves H. Kwan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dicke states are an elementary family of many-body quantum states, consisting of equal superpositions of all configurations of [MATH] qubits with [MATH] excitations. We show that their magic, as measured by the stabilizer R\'enyi entropy (SRE), is extensive at every filling [MATH] except half-filling, and we obtain the magic density analytically, together with the subleading terms. In the context of fault-tolerant quantum computation, we also investigate the yield of Dicke states, and find that they can produce on average an extensive number of CCZ states (or [MATH] states with a catalyst) at any [MATH]. This yield is not self-averaging, but fluctuates from run to run by [MATH], as if it were set by a hidden phase shared by all qubits. At half-filling, the SRE grows only logarithmically, while the preparation cost, average yield and relative entropy of magic remain extensive, so that a small SRE does not necessarily signal a weak resource. These results can be understood by viewing the Dicke state as a fixed-magnetization projection of a product of tilted spins.
tldr: The paper analytically characterizes the magic of Dicke states via stabilizer Rényi entropy and studies their usefulness as a resource for producing CCZ/T states in fault-tolerant quantum computation.
motivation: Dicke states are a basic many-body family, but their non-stabilizerness and resource yield for fault-tolerant quantum computation are not fully understood.
method: The authors compute the stabilizer Rényi entropy (SRE) of Dicke states analytically, including magic density and subleading terms, and analyze preparation cost and magic-state yield, interpreting results via a fixed-magnetization projection of tilted spin products.
result: They find extensive SRE at every filling except half-filling, where SRE grows only logarithmically, while preparation cost, average CCZ-state yield, and relative entropy of magic remain extensive; the yield is not self-averaging and fluctuates extensively.
conclusion: The work shows that small SRE does not necessarily imply a weak magic resource and provides a detailed resource-theoretic characterization of Dicke states relevant to fault-tolerant quantum computation.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper studies the non-stabilizerness (magic) of Dicke states, which are equal superpositions of all L-qubit computational basis states with exactly n excitations (Hamming weight n). Using the stabilizer Rényi entropy (SRE) as the magic measure, the authors prove that the SRE is extensive for all filling fractions f = n/L except f = 1/2. They derive an exact analytic expression for the magic density in the thermodynamic limit, along with subleading corrections. title: Fast Mixing And Thermal Phases From Strong Decay Of Correlations
authors: Vedika Khemani Chao Yin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17433v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that a strong form of correlation decay in quantum Gibbs states has far-reaching dynamical consequences. For a smooth path of geometrically local commuting Hamiltonians whose Gibbs states satisfy strong decay of correlations, we construct [MATH]-time quasi-local Lindbladian evolutions exactly connecting these states in both directions, together with [MATH]-time quasi-local Hamiltonian evolutions exactly connecting their canonical purifications. These quasi-local connections strengthen previously known quantum-channel circuit constructions based on the decay of connected correlation functions [R. Ma, V. Khemani, and S. Sang, PRX Quantum 7, 033052 (2026)], which approximately connect states within the same phase but have depths that grow logarithmically with system size. Furthermore, if the Gibbs-state path contains a product state, we prove that the single-site Glauber dynamics has a [MATH] spectral gap independent of the system size throughout the path. This establishes Glauber-dynamics fast mixing for models that may violate the strong spatial mixing condition used in prior proofs, including (1) the [MATH]-state Potts model throughout the high-temperature phase for any [MATH] and any finite dimension; (2) the Ising model with a longitudinal field at low temperature, with frustrating perturbations that destroy monotonicity of the dynamics; and (3) the three-dimensional [MATH] lattice gauge theory at low temperatures comparing to a field perturbation, even though the model supports classical memories at intermediate temperatures. Intriguingly, we establish fast mixing of these classical Markov chains using tools from quantum physics like Lieb-Robinson bounds.

motivation: Prior circuit constructions connecting Gibbs states via decay of connected correlations only approximately connect states within a phase and have depths growing logarithmically with system size; a stronger dynamical and mixing guarantee was lacking.
method: For geometrically local commuting Hamiltonians along a smooth path with strongly decaying Gibbs-state correlations, the authors construct polynomial-time quasi-local Lindbladian evolutions exactly connecting the Gibbs states and quasi-local Hamiltonian evolutions connecting their canonical purifications; they prove spectral gaps using Lieb-Robinson bounds inspired by quantum tools.
result: Glauber dynamics has a system-size-independent spectral gap throughout paths containing a product state, establishing fast mixing for cases violating strong spatial mixing—including q-state Potts models in the high-temperature phase, Ising with longitudinal field at low temperature with frustrating perturbations, and 3D Z2 lattice gauge theory at low temperature.
conclusion: Strong correlation decay of Gibbs states yields far-reaching dynamical consequences, and quantum-physics tools like Lieb-Robinson bounds can prove fast mixing of classical Markov chains beyond prior strong-spatial-mixing assumptions.

These constructions improve upon previous work by Ma, Khemani, and Sang (PRX Quantum 7, 033052 (2026)), which used decay of connected correlations to build quantum circuits of depth growing logarithmically with system size that approximately connect states within the same phase. The new results achieve exact connections with constant depth (quasi-local) by leveraging the stronger correlation decay and the commuting nature of the Hamiltonians.

A key consequence is that if the Gibbs-state path contains a product state, then the single-site Glauber dynamics for the corresponding classical Markov chain has a spectral gap that is Ω(1) uniformly in system size. This proves fast mixing for several important models that were not covered by previous techniques based on strong spatial mixing. title: The Radical Pair Mechanism Can Generate Nuclear-spin Entanglement
authors: Rishabh, Hadi Zadeh-Haghighi, Christoph Simon
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17497v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The radical pair mechanism is a quantum-mechanical process underlying weak magnetic field effects in chemical and biological systems. While nuclear polarization and electronic entanglement in this mechanism have been studied extensively, the possibility of creating entanglement between nuclear spins has, to the best of our knowledge, remained unexplored. Here, we show that nuclear-spin entanglement can develop from initially maximally mixed nuclear spin states and evolve over repeated radical pair cycles. Its generation and persistence depend on the initial electronic state, the available reaction channels, and the interplay between recombination rates, hyperfine interactions, and the magnetic field. We demonstrate this behaviour in both a minimal two-nucleus model and a five-nucleus model inspired by the photosynthetic radical pair P700--[MATH]. Radical pair mechanism generated nuclear-spin entanglement offers a potential new resource for quantum technologies and opens avenues for exploring its role in biological systems.

motivation: Radical pair mechanisms are known to produce electronic entanglement and nuclear polarization, but nuclear-spin entanglement had remained largely unexplored as a possible resource.
method: The authors model radical pair dynamics with hyperfine interactions, recombination rates, reaction channels, and magnetic field effects in a minimal two-nucleus model and a five-nucleus model inspired by the photosynthetic P700 radical pair.
result: Nuclear-spin entanglement develops from initially mixed states and its generation and persistence depend on the initial electronic state, reaction channels, and the interplay between recombination, hyperfine coupling, and magnetic fields.
conclusion: Radical-pair-generated nuclear-spin entanglement may provide a new resource for quantum technologies and could play a role in biological systems.

title: Finite-time Spectral Enhancement Of Transient Quantum Thermometry
authors: M. Tahir Naseem, Asghar Ullah, \"ozg\"ur E. M\"ustecapl\i O\u{g}lu, Mehmet Cengiz Onba\c{s}l\i
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17522v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transient quantum thermometry extracts temperature information before a probe reaches thermal equilibrium. We study how finite interaction times affect thermometric precision for a harmonic-oscillator probe prepared in a number state and weakly coupled to a thermal bosonic reservoir. A second-order time-convolutionless master equation retains the finite-time reservoir response, allowing modes away from the probe frequency to shape the populations and their temperature dependence. For the baseline parameters, this response raises the quantum Fisher information about fivefold above the Markovian prediction, in agreement with an exact solution of the model. When the probability of leaving the initial state is small, we derive an analytical condition for this enhancement. To assess its operational significance, we examine the temperature information acquired per unit time. Under the exact dynamics, this rate is largest within the reservoir memory time. With negligible preparation and readout overhead, the optimum is about five times the best Markovian rate and 30 times an upper bound on the equilibrium rate. The advantage survives smooth switching, although overhead and longer coupling ramps reduce it.
tldr: The paper analyzes finite-time enhancement of transient quantum thermometry for a harmonic-oscillator probe weakly coupled to a thermal bosonic reservoir.
motivation: Transient thermometry aims to extract temperature information before equilibration, but finite interaction times and reservoir memory effects are usually neglected in Markovian treatments.

result: For baseline parameters, finite-time reservoir response raises the quantum Fisher information about fivefold over the Markovian prediction, and the temperature-information rate can be about five times the best Markovian rate and 30 times an equilibrium upper bound.
conclusion: Finite-time reservoir memory can significantly improve transient thermometric precision, though preparation/readout overhead and longer coupling ramps reduce the advantage.

title: DRAG-Inspired Single Flux Quantum Control Of Superconducting Qubits
authors: V. Vozhakov, M. Bastrakova, A. Liniov, D. Kulandin, N. Klenov, I. Soloviev
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17562v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scalable control remains a major challenge for superconducting quantum processors due to the wiring, thermal load, and hardware complexity associated with conventional microwave-based architectures. A framework for qubit control based on Single Flux Quantum (SFQ) digital electronics is presented. For transmon qubits, optimized control sequences are constructed from regular pulse trains framed by arbitrary subsequences (ramps), enabling DRAG-inspired leakage suppression in the discrete SFQ regime through genetic-algorithm optimization. For representative [MATH] gates, the resulting sequences achieve simulated coherent-control infidelities below [MATH], including leakage from the computational subspace. The objective of the proposed approach is to demonstrate that coherent errors intrinsic to SFQ control can be reduced to a comparable level for a more scalable cryogenic control architecture. Memory requirements are reduced by storing only the optimized ramps, while a modular controller architecture supporting both regular and arbitrary pulse generation is proposed. The logical complexity of this architecture is estimated from the Josephson-junction counts of its constituent SFQ cells. The proposed approach therefore combines low coherent-control error with reduced memory overhead and provides a basis for scalable cryogenic SFQ control architectures.
tldr: The paper proposes a DRAG-inspired Single Flux Quantum control framework for superconducting transmon qubits, using genetic-algorithm-optimized pulse sequences to suppress leakage and reduce coherent-control errors.
motivation: Conventional microwave control of superconducting qubits faces scalability limits due to wiring, thermal load, and hardware complexity, motivating cryogenic digital control architectures such as SFQ electronics.
method: Optimized control sequences are constructed from regular SFQ pulse trains with arbitrary ramp subsequences, and a genetic algorithm is used to achieve DRAG-inspired leakage suppression in the discrete SFQ regime.
result: For representative gates, the optimized sequences achieve simulated coherent-control infidelities below a target threshold, including leakage outside the computational subspace, while reducing memory requirements by storing only optimized ramps.
conclusion: The approach combines low coherent-control error with reduced memory overhead and provides a basis for scalable cryogenic SFQ control architectures for superconducting quantum processors.

title: Multitime Equilibration And Multitime Mpemba Effects
authors: He Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Equilibration of a quantum state leaves open whether its response to later interventions has also equilibrated. We establish multitime equilibration for a continuous process on a fixed observation window, retaining the autonomous system--environment dynamics and all internal time differences. A finite-time mean-square bound controls the full continuous-process norm through the effective energy dimension and energy-gap correlations. A factorial temporal-order bound lifts fixed-sector convergence to the full process, while a process-visible spectral measure distinguishes mean-square from pointwise equilibration. This framework defines multitime Mpemba effects by comparing preparations relative to one stationary process. In a semicircle-spectrum model, a preparation filter changes the decay exponent from [MATH] to [MATH] in every fixed sector and in the summed norm, despite a larger initial distance. A fixed unitary control and terminal measurement exhibit the same exponent improvement in their output probabilities. Noncommuting baths and a many-body spin environment separate this all-sector mechanism from selective finite-time acceleration.
tldr: The paper establishes a multitime equilibration framework for continuous quantum processes and uses it to define and analyze multitime Mpemba effects.
motivation: Equilibration of a quantum state does not guarantee that its later response to interventions has equilibrated, so a multitime formulation is needed to characterize full process equilibration and temporal acceleration phenomena.
method: The author derives finite-time mean-square bounds controlled by effective energy dimension and energy-gap correlations, proves a factorial temporal-order bound, and introduces a process-visible spectral measure to distinguish mean-square from pointwise equilibration.
result: In a semicircle-spectrum model, a preparation filter improves the decay exponent in every fixed sector and in the summed norm, and the same exponent improvement appears in output probabilities under fixed unitary control and terminal measurement.
conclusion: The framework separates an all-sector multitime Mpemba mechanism from selective finite-time acceleration and clarifies how noncommuting baths and many-body spin environments affect multitime equilibration.

They establish a finite-time mean-square bound that controls the norm of the full continuous process in terms of the effective energy dimension and energy-gap correlations. A factorial temporal-order bound is derived to lift convergence from fixed sectors (defined by temporal orderings) to the full process, and a process-visible spectral measure is introduced to distinguish mean-square from pointwise equilibration. The framework is used to define multitime Mpemba effects by comparing different preparations relative to one stationary process. In a semicircle-spectrum model, a preparation filter is shown to change the decay exponent from 3/2 to 5/2 in every fixed sector and in the summed norm, despite a larger initial distance. A fixed unitary control and terminal measurement exhibit the same exponent improvement in output probabilities. Noncommuting baths and a many-body spin environment are used to separate this all-sector mechanism from selective finite-time acceleration.

title: Reference-Assisted Qutrit Control And Conditional One-Round Distillation In A Charge-4e Superconductor Model
authors: Wang Junhao (eigen)
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formulate a charge-[MATH] parafermionic-vortex route to qutrit processing as a conditional theory with explicit operational assumptions. Sector preservation and same-label charge-conjugation covariance imply closure for every adaptive visible record. For charge-conjugation-invariant inputs, record probabilities are independent of the supported reference state; for arbitrary inputs, discarding the reference gives a population-weighted mixture of conjugate sector maps. We give a finite-depth stability bound for complete labelled instruments, including postselection and initial zero-sector contamination. A self-contained calculation reproduces the known dense single-qutrit closure of the registered Clifford-plus-Flip gate set. We also specify an abstract ternary CSS [MATH] syndrome/recovery decoder: 243 classical representatives per CSS component correct all 3,609 Pauli errors of support weight at most two, and an exact integer dynamic program yields the full independent-Pauli logical enumerator. Its all-syndrome acceptance is distinct from the known [MATH] ideal acceptance of one-round strange-state Golay distillation. An accepted-run target-infidelity budget and a synthetic parameter protocol expose the remaining noise assumptions. Native charge-[MATH] syndrome extraction, material feasibility, a device threshold, and unconditional fault tolerance are not established.
tldr: The paper develops a conditional charge-4e parafermionic-vortex framework for qutrit control, reference-assisted sector maps, and a ternary CSS decoder relevant to one-round distillation.
motivation: It aims to connect qutrit processing and conditional distillation to a concrete charge-4e superconductor platform while making operational assumptions explicit.
method: The authors formulate sector-preserving qutrit operations with charge-conjugation covariance, derive stability bounds for labelled instruments, reproduce Clifford-plus-Flip closure, and specify a ternary CSS syndrome/recovery decoder with logical enumerator calculations.
result: They show closure for adaptive visible records, reference-state dependence for invariant inputs, correction of all weight-<=2 Pauli errors by the proposed decoder, and distinguish its all-syndrome acceptance from Golay-distillation acceptance.
conclusion: The work provides a conditional qutrit-processing and distillation-oriented error-correction analysis, but does not establish native syndrome extraction, material feasibility, a device threshold, or unconditional fault tolerance.

title: Benchmarking Superconducting Quantum Processors With Percolating Entanglement Quality
authors: Akinori Machino, Kazuhisa Ogawa, Takefumi Miyoshi, Hidehisa Shiomi, Shinichi Morisaka, Ryo Matsuda, Nilton F. G. Filho, Koichiro Ban, Takafumi Miyanaga, Keisuke Koike, Ryutaro Ohira, Toshi Sumida, Yoshinori Kurimoto, Yuuya Sugita, Yosuke Ito, Yasunari Suzuki, Peter A. Spring, Shiyu Wang, Hiroto Mukai, Arvind Mamgain, Shuhei Tamate, Yutaka Tabuchi, Yasunobu Nakamura, Makoto Negoro
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The capability to create large entanglement resources is a key performance attribute of quantum processors, and the size of the resource is often used as a benchmark of processor scale. Recent graph-state experiments have reported entanglement clusters spanning entire chips with hundreds of qubits. However, cluster size alone does not capture the entanglement quality of individual couplings or differences in coupling topology. Here, we introduce percolating entanglement quality (PEQ), a topology-normalized benchmark based on conditional two-qubit negativity and a topology-specific bond-percolation threshold. As an experimental demonstration, we prepare a native graph state on a 64-qubit square-lattice superconducting processor with defects, identify a 52-qubit entanglement cluster, and evaluate the PEQ of the processor. Applying PEQ to previously reported chip-wide graph-state measurements on heavy-hex-lattice processors, we show that PEQ differs substantially among processors whose entanglement clusters span the entire chip. PEQ provides a single chip-wide score without selecting a best-performing qubit subset or path. This score allows processors with different coupling topologies to be compared on a common scale and can inform the design of coupling topologies for scalable chips.
tldr: The paper introduces percolating entanglement quality (PEQ), a topology-normalized benchmark for graph-state entanglement on superconducting quantum processors.
motivation: Cluster size alone does not capture entanglement quality or coupling-topology differences, so a chip-wide benchmark is needed to compare processors fairly.
method: PEQ is defined using conditional two-qubit negativity and a topology-specific bond-percolation threshold; it is demonstrated on a 64-qubit square-lattice superconducting processor with defects and applied to heavy-hex-lattice data.
result: The authors identify a 52-qubit entanglement cluster and show that PEQ distinguishes processors whose entanglement clusters span the entire chip, enabling comparison across different coupling topologies.
conclusion: PEQ provides a single chip-wide entanglement-quality score that can inform coupling-topology design for scalable superconducting processors.

title: QuantumInputOutput.jl: A Julia Framework For Input-output Theory With Quantum Pulses And The Slh Formalism
authors: Christoph Hotter, Orjan Ameye, Klaus M{\o}lmer
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17451v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The interaction of traveling photonic pulses with quantum systems is a fundamental process for many quantum technologies such as quantum communication, control, and measurement protocols. The so-called SLH formalism, named for the triple of operators that parametrize the dynamics, in combination with virtual emission and absorption cavities provides a general toolbox to describe such processes. However, modeling open quantum systems driven by propagating quantum pulses becomes cumbersome once several components, channels, and temporal modes are involved. Here we present QuantumInputOutput.jl, an open-source framework that automates this derivation process: first, symbolic expressions for the Hamiltonian and Lindblad operators are derived using predefined SLH rules and symbolic quantum algebra. Next, the obtained operators are converted to (time-dependent) numerical matrices or are used to obtain higher-order mean-field equations. The numerical expressions are presented in a form immediately suitable for solving the time evolution of the master equation and analyzing the output modes via correlation functions. Besides its usefulness for numerical simulations, the framework also provides a convenient tool to derive symbolic expressions for one-dimensional quantum systems such as multilevel emitters in cavities or waveguides.
tldr: QuantumInputOutput.jl is an open-source Julia framework that automates SLH-based modeling and simulation of open quantum systems driven by propagating quantum pulses.
motivation: Modeling traveling photonic pulses interacting with quantum systems becomes cumbersome when multiple components, channels, and temporal modes are involved, especially for quantum communication, control, and measurement protocols.
method: The framework uses symbolic SLH rules and quantum algebra to derive Hamiltonians and Lindblad operators, then converts them into time-dependent numerical matrices or higher-order mean-field equations suitable for master-equation evolution and output-mode correlation analysis.
result: It provides a practical tool for both numerical simulations and symbolic derivations of one-dimensional quantum systems such as multilevel emitters in cavities or waveguides.
conclusion: The work is a useful modeling and simulation framework for pulse-driven open quantum systems, particularly relevant to waveguide/cavity/emitter platforms, but it does not present a new physical protocol or experimental result.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces QuantumInputOutput.jl, an open-source Julia framework for modeling open quantum systems driven by traveling photonic pulses. The core problem addressed is the complexity of deriving the quantum stochastic dynamics for such systems when multiple components, channels, and temporal modes are involved. The authors leverage the SLH (Scattering, Lindblad, Hamiltonian) formalism, which provides a compositional way to describe quantum input-output networks, combined with virtual emission and absorption cavities to handle propagating pulses. The framework automates the derivation of symbolic expressions for the Hamiltonian and Lindblad operators using predefined SLH rules and symbolic quantum algebra. These symbolic expressions are then converted into time-dependent numerical matrices or used to generate higher-order mean-field equations. title: Linear Monitoring-feedback Model For Linearized Gravity
authors: Daisuke Miki, Alfred Li, Yiqiu Ma, Yubao Liu, Yanbei Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17642v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether gravity has quantum degrees of freedom is a question of fundamental importance. We formulate a linear monitoring-feedback framework for gravitational interactions that includes local classical-record models of semiclassical gravity and, when quantum resources are supplied in correlated ancilla inputs, can reproduce linearized quantum-gravity dynamics. Auxiliary systems monitor the positions of massive bodies, and their records are fed back through a chosen gravitational response kernel. At the level of linear input-output theory, this construction makes the deterministic response explicit while exposing the force noise and correlations associated with the auxiliary sector. We organize the allowed ancilla correlations into three regimes. In Regime-I, independent ancillas have unsqueezed, uncorrelated sensing and back-action quadratures. A single object then has a minimum classical-gravity noise (CGN), S_F^min = 2 hbar M Omega_SN^2, where Omega_SN is the Schrodinger-Newton frequency set by the microscopic mass distribution. In Regime-II, arbitrary local sensing--back-action correlations are allowed, but the ancillas associated with different objects remain independent. The single-object CGN is then unrestricted, while the joint force-noise matrix obeys a determinant bound that is equivalent to the local classical-channel/no-entanglement bound. In Regime-III, cross-object correlations and a common nonlocal mediator are allowed. The commuting force noises can then be jointly squeezed, entanglement between the masses can occur, and--with a suitable retarded response and input state--the monitoring-feedback system can reproduce the noise and commutators of linearized quantum gravity, including non-Markovian quantum fluctuations.
tldr: A linear monitoring-feedback model distinguishes classical-record semiclassical gravity from linearized quantum gravity via ancilla-correlation regimes, force-noise bounds, and mass entanglement.
motivation: The paper addresses whether gravity has quantum degrees of freedom by contrasting classical-record models with quantum-gravity dynamics in a linear input-output framework.
method: Auxiliary systems monitor massive-body positions and feed records back through a gravitational response kernel; allowed ancilla correlations are organized into three regimes and analyzed using linear input-output noise and commutator bounds.
result: Regime-I yields a minimum classical-gravity noise, Regime-II gives a determinant bound equivalent to a local classical-channel/no-entanglement condition, and Regime-III with cross-object correlations can jointly squeeze force noise, entangle masses, and reproduce linearized quantum-gravity fluctuations.
conclusion: Monitoring-feedback with controlled ancilla correlations provides a unified linear framework to separate classical and quantum gravitational mediators and to model non-Markovian quantum gravitational noise.

title: Beyond Blossom: Accelerating Mwpm Decoding For Surface Codes With Local Predecoding And Architecture-Aware Optimizations
authors: Jiayu Fu, Zirong Shen, Lin Gan, Yiming Zhang, Wenjing Han, Xiaoming Sun, Riling Li, Guangwen Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) is widely used to decode surface codes, but its computational cost increases with code distance. We present Beyond Blossom, a state-of-the-art CPU-based MWPM decoder for surface codes. It combines algorithmic optimization through local predecoding, architecture-aware optimization, and pipeline-wide parallelism to reduce matching workload and execution overhead while preserving MWPM optimality. Across rotated surface codes with distances 9-33 and circuit-level physical error rates of 0.05%-0.3%, on a single CPU core, Beyond Blossom achieves a 4.23[MATH] geometric-mean speedup and up to 5.58[MATH] speedup over Sparse Blossom in PyMatching. At distance 33 and a physical error rate of 0.1%, with 8 CPU cores, decoding a block of 33 measurement rounds takes 21.40 [MATH]s on average, equivalent to 0.65 [MATH]s per round.
tldr: The paper presents Beyond Blossom, a CPU-based MWPM decoder for surface codes that uses local predecoding and architecture-aware optimizations to significantly speed up decoding while preserving MWPM optimality.

method: The authors combine local predecoding to reduce the matching problem size, architecture-aware CPU optimizations, and pipeline-wide parallelism to accelerate MWPM without sacrificing optimality.
result: For rotated surface codes with distances 9-33 and circuit-level error rates 0.05%-0.3%, Beyond Blossom achieves a 4.23x geometric-mean speedup and up to 5.58x speedup over Sparse Blossom in PyMatching on a single CPU core; at distance 33 and 0.1% error, it decodes a 33-round block in about 21.40 microseconds using 8 cores.
conclusion: Beyond Blossom provides a state-of-the-art practical CPU decoder for surface codes, showing that algorithmic and architecture-aware optimizations can substantially improve MWPM decoding performance for quantum error correction.

title: Underlying Orbital U(1) Symmetry In Quantum Limit Cycles
authors: Chong Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum limit cycles exhibit harmonic Liouvillian spectra, yet their underlying orbital [MATH] structure is not generally explicit in the absence of physical rotational symmetry. Here, we construct a unitary representation of orbital phase translations through a similarity transformation that maps the harmonic nondecaying Liouvillian sector onto a Hermitian angular-momentum Hamiltonian. The resulting phase states possess homogeneous Fubini--Study geometry independently of the physical orbit's shape. For ideal quantum limit cycles, the corresponding density matrix also exhibit homogeneous Bures geometry. At finite size, we show how phase diffusion damps slow Liouvillian harmonics while preserving the effective orbital [MATH] symmetry. The resulting loss of phase-state distinguishability and contraction of the effective geometry are quantitatively predicted by the microscopic slow Liouvillian spectrum. Our results establish a connection between orbital phase symmetry, quantum geometry, and finite-size phase diffusion in open quantum systems.
tldr: The paper constructs an effective orbital U(1) symmetry for quantum limit cycles by mapping the nondecaying Liouvillian sector to an angular-momentum Hamiltonian, and analyzes how finite-size phase diffusion degrades phase-state distinguishability and quantum geometry.
motivation: Quantum limit cycles have harmonic Liouvillian spectra, but their orbital phase structure is usually implicit unless the system has physical rotational symmetry. The work aims to expose this structure and connect it to phase diffusion in open quantum systems.
method: The author uses a similarity transformation to unitarily represent orbital phase translations, mapping the harmonic nondecaying Liouvillian sector onto a Hermitian angular-momentum Hamiltonian. Phase states and their Fubini-Study/Bures geometries are then analyzed for ideal and finite-size limit cycles.
result: Ideal quantum limit cycles yield phase states with homogeneous Fubini-Study geometry and density matrices with homogeneous Bures geometry, independent of orbit shape. At finite size, slow Liouvillian harmonics are damped by phase diffusion while an effective orbital U(1) symmetry persists, with geometry contraction and loss of distinguishability predicted by the slow Liouvillian spectrum.
conclusion: The results link orbital phase symmetry, quantum geometry, and finite-size phase diffusion in open quantum systems, providing a framework for understanding phase coherence in quantum limit cycles beyond systems with explicit rotational symmetry.

The work thus connects orbital phase symmetry, quantum geometric tensors, and finite-size phase diffusion in open quantum systems.

title: Indefinite Causal Order With Definite Bohmian Trajectories For The Quantum Switch
authors: Aur\'elien Drezet
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze the notion of indefinite causal order (ICO) from the standpoint of the deterministic de Broglie--Bohm theory, based on the notion of trajectories in configuration space. More precisely, we study the physics of the quantum switch (QS) interferometer within a Bohmian framework and show how the notion of causality is preserved in this approach. Furthermore, we investigate device-independent certification and causal inequalities applied to an entangled quantum system, and show that in this regime too, the notions of trajectories and of a strict causal order are perfectly preserved.
tldr: The paper analyzes the quantum switch and indefinite causal order within the de Broglie–Bohm pilot-wave theory, arguing that definite Bohmian trajectories preserve a strict causal order even in this ICO scenario.
motivation: Indefinite causal order challenges conventional notions of causality, and the author aims to show how a deterministic hidden-variable interpretation can reconcile the quantum switch with a well-defined causal structure.
method: The author applies the de Broglie–Bohm theory to the quantum switch interferometer, examining trajectories in configuration space, and also considers device-independent certification and causal inequalities for an entangled quantum system.
result: The analysis finds that Bohmian trajectories provide a definite causal ordering in the quantum switch, and that strict causal order is preserved in the entangled device-independent setting as well.
conclusion: The paper concludes that indefinite causal order need not imply a fundamental breakdown of causality when viewed through Bohmian mechanics, suggesting a compatible interpretation of ICO phenomena.

They argue that the apparent indeterminacy of causal order in the QS arises from the wavefunction's superposition, while the Bohmian trajectories always follow a well-defined sequence of interactions. Furthermore, the paper extends the analysis to device-independent certification and causal inequalities applied to entangled quantum systems, demonstrating that the notions of trajectories and strict causal order remain intact in these scenarios as well. The authors conclude that ICO does not imply a fundamental violation of causality but rather reflects the wavefunction's nonlocal structure, which is compatible with a deterministic, causal description at the hidden-variable level.

For the device-independent and causal inequality scenarios, they consider entangled states and analyze the trajectories of particles in Bell-type experiments, showing that the observed correlations can be reproduced by a causal model with hidden variables (the Bohmian positions). The methodology is primarily interpretive and analytical, relying on exact solutions of the Bohmian dynamics for idealized setups rather than numerical simulations or experimental data.

The authors show that the trajectory does not exhibit any superposition of causal orders; instead, the order is fixed for each individual run, and the ensemble statistics reproduce the quantum predictions. title: Analytic Spread Complexity In Three-level Systems And The Spacing-ratio Distribution
authors: Pratik Nandy
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17417v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The spread complexity characterizes the spreading of a quantum state over the Krylov basis and has been proposed to capture the correlations between energy levels. How such correlations manifest in the dynamics has been studied mainly numerically for large matrices. Here we consider three-level systems, the smallest setting with spacing correlations, and derive exact results for the spread complexity, the Krylov variance, and the Krylov entropy. At infinite temperature, the Krylov basis depends on the spectrum only through the ratio of consecutive level spacings, and the spectral variance enters only as an overall time scale. For Gaussian ensembles, these variables are statistically independent, and the averaged spread complexity and variance reduce to one-dimensional integrals over the spacing-ratio distribution encoding the level statistics. We establish universal late-time values of the complexity and variance, and an algebraic relaxation with exponents set by the Dyson index. We also outline the extension to [MATH] levels, with the ensemble-averaged spread complexity expressed as a [MATH]-dimensional integral over the joint distribution of consecutive spacing ratios.
tldr: The paper analytically derives spread complexity, Krylov variance, and Krylov entropy for three-level systems, relating them to level-spacing-ratio statistics and Dyson-index-dependent relaxation.
motivation: Spread complexity has been proposed as a probe of energy-level correlations, but most studies rely on numerical treatments of large random matrices; small systems with exact analytic results are lacking.
method: The authors compute the Krylov basis and spread complexity for three-level systems at infinite temperature, showing that the spectrum enters through consecutive level-spacing ratios and an overall time scale, then average over Gaussian ensembles using the spacing-ratio distribution.
result: They obtain exact expressions and universal late-time values for the spread complexity and Krylov variance, along with algebraic relaxation exponents determined by the Dyson index, and outline an extension to M-level systems via joint spacing-ratio distributions.
conclusion: The work provides a rare analytic link between spread complexity and random-matrix level statistics in the smallest setting with spacing correlations, offering a template for higher-dimensional extensions.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper investigates the spread complexity of quantum states in three-level systems, which are the smallest systems exhibiting level spacing correlations. The authors derive exact analytical results for the spread complexity, Krylov variance, and Krylov entropy at infinite temperature. They show that the Krylov basis depends on the spectrum only through the ratio of consecutive level spacings, while the overall spectral variance sets a time scale. For Gaussian ensembles (GOE, GUE, GSE), these variables are statistically independent, allowing the averaged spread complexity and variance to be expressed as one-dimensional integrals over the spacing-ratio distribution. The authors establish universal late-time values for complexity and variance, and find an algebraic relaxation with exponents determined by the Dyson index. They also outline an extension to d-level systems, where the ensemble-averaged spread complexity becomes a (d-2)-dimensional integral over the joint distribution of consecutive spacing ratios.
key_contributions: Exact analytical derivation of spread complexity, Krylov variance, and Krylov entropy for three-level systems at infinite temperature.

Proof that for Gaussian ensembles the spacing ratios and spectral variance are statistically independent, reducing ensemble averages to one-dimensional integrals over the spacing-ratio distribution.
Establishment of universal late-time values for spread complexity and variance, and identification of algebraic relaxation exponents set by the Dyson index.
Extension of the framework to d-level systems, expressing the ensemble-averaged spread complexity as a (d-2)-dimensional integral over the joint distribution of consecutive spacing ratios.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ the Krylov basis construction via the Lanczos algorithm for a three-level system, which yields a tridiagonal Hamiltonian. They analytically compute the spread complexity, defined as the sum of the probabilities of occupying Krylov basis states weighted by their index, as well as the Krylov variance and entropy. By considering Gaussian ensembles (GOE, GUE, GSE), they exploit the known joint probability distribution of energy levels to derive the distribution of consecutive spacing ratios. The key methodological step is the factorization of the ensemble average into an integral over the spacing ratio and an independent average over the overall spectral scale, justified by the statistical independence of these variables in Gaussian ensembles. This reduces the problem to one-dimensional integrals that can be evaluated numerically or analytically in limiting cases. The extension to d levels uses a similar factorization but results in higher-dimensional integrals over the joint distribution of consecutive spacing ratios.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper presents exact expressions for the spread complexity, Krylov variance, and Krylov entropy in terms of the spacing ratio r and the spectral variance. For Gaussian ensembles, the averaged quantities are given by one-dimensional integrals over the spacing-ratio distribution P(r). The authors find that at late times, the spread complexity and variance approach universal values that depend only on the Dyson index β (β=1 for GOE, β=2 for GUE, β=4 for GSE). Specifically, the late-time complexity saturates to a constant, while the variance decays algebraically with an exponent determined by β. For example, the relaxation exponent is found to be related to the Dyson index, though the exact numerical values are not explicitly stated in the abstract. The results are derived for infinite temperature; finite-temperature effects are not considered. The d-level extension shows that the ensemble-averaged spread complexity can be expressed as a (d-2)-dimensional integral, providing a systematic way to compute complexity for larger systems.
strengths: Provides exact analytical results for a minimal model (three-level system) that captures essential features of level correlations, offering clear insights into the role of spectral statistics.
Demonstrates a factorization that simplifies ensemble averages, reducing the problem to one-dimensional integrals, which is both elegant and computationally efficient.
Establishes universal late-time behavior and algebraic relaxation with exponents tied to the Dyson index, revealing a direct link between complexity dynamics and symmetry class.
Outlines a systematic extension to d-level systems, suggesting a general framework for higher-dimensional cases.

The three-level system, while minimal, may not capture all features of level correlations present in larger systems, and the extension to d levels involves higher-dimensional integrals that may be challenging to evaluate analytically.
The paper focuses on Gaussian ensembles; other ensembles or realistic systems with non-Gaussian level statistics are not considered, limiting the universality of the conclusions.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum physics, particularly in the study of quantum chaos, random matrix theory, and the dynamics of complex quantum systems. The spread complexity in the Krylov basis is a novel probe of quantum dynamics that connects to operator growth and information scrambling. The exact results for three-level systems provide a benchmark for understanding how spectral correlations influence complexity growth, which is valuable for researchers exploring quantum chaos and thermalization. The universal late-time behavior and dependence on the Dyson index offer insights into symmetry classification and may inspire further studies in higher-dimensional systems or with finite-temperature effects.

The factorization of ensemble averages and the identification of universal late-time behavior are significant contributions.
