The novelty lies in the analytical tractability of the three-level system and the explicit connection to the Dyson index, which will be of interest to the quantum chaos and random matrix theory communities.

title: Quantum Data Processing Unit For Neutral-Atom Quantum Computers
authors: Pranav Srinivas Murali, Russell Marroquin Solares, Warren Zhou, Wanda Hou, Anil Bilgin, Yi-Zhuang You
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17652v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computers need real-time classical processing to convert measurement data into feedback within device-specific timing constraints. We introduce the quantum data processing unit (QDPU), an architecture between a quantum device and its controller. Its core is a machine-learned quantum data model (QDM), adapted to the measurement response and noise characteristics of the device. We implement an FPGA pipeline for neutral-atom array assembly that performs occupancy detection and rearrangement scheduling in FPGA logic. One calibrated matched-filter lane classifies a [MATH] array in 12.5 [MATH]s. An atom-loss model using a software reference planner evaluates a [MATH] target with a 60 s trap lifetime and 0.1% loss per moved atom. Removing an assumed 150 ms host round trip raises the predicted assembly success from 8% to 85% and reduces the wall-clock time per successful assembly from 19 s to 0.16 s. A GPU-based outer loop is proposed for refitting model parameters between runs. Its NVQLink transport is measured on the board: over 10 GbE to an NVIDIA DGX Spark, the median FPGA-to-host-to-FPGA round trip is 2.74 [MATH]s for 128-byte messages forwarded by a CPU core. A separate 12-bit learned qLDPC kernel is placed and routed for the same FPGA target, with a derived latency of 0.84 ms per round for a [MATH] lifted-product code under code-capacity noise. A quantised GraphMP ranking kernel for the same code runs on the board with a median host-to-FPGA-to-host latency of 50.5 [MATH]s with one shot in flight, excluding host-side BP+OSD post-processing. Together, these implementations illustrate a shared architecture with workload-specific models and timing requirements.
tldr: Introduces a quantum data processing unit architecture with machine-learned models and FPGA/GPU kernels for real-time classical processing in neutral-atom quantum computers.
motivation: Neutral-atom quantum computers require low-latency classical processing to convert measurement data into feedback and to schedule atom rearrangement within device-specific timing constraints.
method: The authors implement an FPGA pipeline for occupancy detection and rearrangement scheduling, use a calibrated matched-filter lane and atom-loss model, measure NVQLink transport latency, and place-and-route qLDPC and GraphMP kernels for the same FPGA target.
result: The FPGA classifies a 2D array in 12.5 microseconds, removing an assumed 150 ms host round trip raises predicted assembly success from 8% to 85% and reduces wall-clock time per successful assembly from 19 s to 0.16 s, and the qLDPC kernel has derived latency of 0.84 ms per round.
conclusion: The work illustrates a shared real-time classical processing architecture for neutral-atom quantum computers, but it is primarily an engineering/control-stack contribution rather than a quantum-information or thermodynamic result.

title: Probing Spatiotemporal Quantum Correlations With Two-Qubit Relaxometry
authors: Christina Psaroudaki
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17509v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum impurities and spin qubits are powerful local probes of magnetic fluctuations, but conventional relaxometry reduces their information to a local relaxation rate at a single frequency. Building on advances in two-qubit sensing of spatial correlations, we show how two complementary protocols probe finite-time correlations in interacting quantum matter. Phase-cycled Bell-state relaxometry isolates the signed contribution of correlated relaxation to the joint ground-state population. To second order in the probe-environment coupling, the resulting population contrast measures a finite-time integral of the energy-ordered cross-correlator. In the longitudinal regime, XY8 covariance probes the complementary symmetrized cross-correlator within a tunable frequency window. For a gapless quantum spin chain, the signals reveal interaction-dependent algebraic scaling and ballistic propagation. Luttinger-liquid theory links sign changes as the qubit frequency is swept to the propagation time between the probes. It also predicts distinct spatial power laws for the Bell signal before the correlation front and at late times, when the sensing window resolves the qubit frequency. Matrix-product-state calculations for the spin chain test the pre-front scaling at zero and finite magnetization and extract the propagation velocity from Bell oscillations at zero magnetization. The probe coupling geometry determines which spin and momentum sectors contribute to the measured signals.
tldr: The paper proposes two-qubit relaxometry protocols to probe finite-time spatiotemporal quantum correlations in interacting quantum matter.
motivation: Conventional single-qubit relaxometry reduces information to a local relaxation rate at one frequency, missing spatial and temporal correlation information.
method: Phase-cycled Bell-state relaxometry isolates signed correlated relaxation, while XY8 covariance probes the symmetrized cross-correlator; the protocols are analyzed with Luttinger-liquid theory and matrix-product-state calculations for a gapless spin chain.
result: The signals reveal interaction-dependent algebraic scaling and ballistic propagation, with sign changes linked to propagation time and distinct spatial power laws before the correlation front and at late times.
conclusion: Two-qubit relaxometry offers a route to characterize spatiotemporal quantum correlations in many-body systems, with probe geometry determining which spin and momentum sectors contribute.

title: Local Gluing Classification And Bulk-locked Clock Rings For $\mathbb{Z}_N$ Models On A Klein Bottle
authors: Wang Junhao (eigen)
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17816v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We classify local reflection gluings of the [MATH] plaquette model on lattice Klein bottles and solve the obstructed literal seam. Within the monomial far-corner ansatz, all commuting gluings form a family labelled by a unit [MATH] of [MATH]. They exist for every [MATH] at even seam length and, at odd length, exactly when [MATH] is a square modulo [MATH]. We determine the anyon transport, including exchange seams with [MATH] for charge conjugation [MATH], and the relation phases that distinguish an unfrustrated code from a commuting but frustrated Hamiltonian. For the literal gluing, the [MATH] noncommuting plaquettes form self-dual clock rings whose sectors are locked by the bulk. This gives an exact reduction of the spectrum to clock-ring spectra, closed-form ring ground energies for [MATH], and a closed-form ground-state degeneracy. We further determine twisted-coefficient homology on the stated surface domains and compare it with logical modules on registered lattice grids; composite dimensions need not give squares of cyclic groups. Dressed-isometry gates and monodromy are reported with their finite-grid scope. Finally, the qudit Gottesman--Knill theorem bounds the computational interpretation: Clifford deformations and Weyl measurements with stabilizer inputs and no external magic states cannot supply a non-stabilizer resource. Charge-conjugation measurements that do supply such states lie outside this operation model. The new results concern explicit seam classification, phase-sensitive consistency and bulk-locked spectra, not a new general no-go theorem or a universal computing architecture.
tldr: The paper classifies local reflection gluings of Z_N plaquette (topological stabilizer) models on lattice Klein bottles and analyses the resulting anyon transport, frustrated phases, and bulk-locked clock-ring spectra.
motivation: Understanding how local seams and non-trivial spatial topology (Klein bottle) affect stabilizer-code consistency, anyon transport, and ground-state degeneracy is relevant for topological quantum codes, but the specific gluing classification is a narrow, model-specific question.
method: Monomial far-corner ansatz for commuting reflection gluings, labelled by a unit of Z_N, combined with anyon-transport/exchange-seam analysis, twisted-coefficient homology on the stated surface domains, and a qudit Gottesman-Knill bound on the computational interpretation.
result: Commuting gluings exist for every N at even seam length and exactly when N is a square mod something at odd length; the noncommuting literal gluing yields self-dual clock rings whose sectors are bulk-locked, giving closed-form ring ground energies, an exact spectral reduction, and a closed-form ground-state degeneracy.
conclusion: The contribution is an explicit seam classification, phase-sensitive consistency conditions, and bulk-locked spectra for Z_N models on Klein bottles, explicitly not a new general no-go theorem or a universal computing architecture; its relevance to the broader quantum-information agenda is specialised.

title: Hybrid Uncertainty In The Real Forms Of $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb C)$
authors: Xiaoli Hu, Xiaoyong Yang, Naihuan Jing
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An optimized commutator bound can lie strictly below the quantum infimum even when its minimizing mean is realized by a quantum state. We study hybrid uncertainty, defined as the sum of pairwise products of standard deviations. For any spanning list of nonzero real linear combinations of the generators in a positive discrete series representation of [MATH], the commutator bound has a unique minimizing mean, realized by a Perelomov coherent state. We prove that the optimized bound equals the infimum over states with finite second moments if and only if the symmetrized covariance matrix of the prescribed observables is diagonal in this state. When this condition fails, the quantum infimum is strictly greater than the bound; for a nonorthogonal list, we obtain an explicit positive lower bound on this gap. For irreducible spin-[MATH] representations of [MATH], we derive the exact minimum of the spectral hybrid uncertainty over states for any spanning list of spin observables. For a fixed state, we compare separate measurements made before a random target is disclosed with direct measurement of the target known in advance. For these protocols, the excess mean squared error coefficient equals twice the listed hybrid uncertainty, and its minimum over orthogonal combinations of the observables equals twice the spectral hybrid uncertainty.
tldr: The paper analyzes hybrid uncertainty relations for real forms of sl(2,C), comparing optimized commutator bounds with the true quantum infimum and deriving exact spectral minima for spin observables.
motivation: Uncertainty relations are fundamental in quantum theory, but optimized commutator bounds can fail to equal the actual state-dependent quantum infimum, so a sharper understanding of when and by how much they differ is needed.
method: The authors study hybrid uncertainty as sums of pairwise standard-deviation products for spanning lists of real linear combinations of generators, use Perelomov coherent states to characterize minimizing means, and derive exact minima for irreducible spin representations and measurement protocols.
result: They prove the optimized commutator bound equals the quantum infimum iff the symmetrized covariance matrix is diagonal in the minimizing coherent state, and otherwise obtain explicit positive lower bounds on the gap; exact spectral hybrid uncertainty minima are derived for spin observables.
conclusion: The work clarifies the structure of uncertainty relations in sl(2,C) representations and quantifies when commutator bounds are tight versus strictly below the true quantum infimum, with implications for measurement-error comparisons.

title: Tight Quantum Query Bounds For Collision Finding Over Arbitrary Bounded Types
authors: Tianci Peng, Shiqi Hou, Xiaoyang Dong
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We determine the bounded-error quantum query complexity of finding one [MATH]-collision in an [MATH]-input function of prescribed type, which specifies all equality-class sizes. For every fixed maximum class size and collision order, we give a tight bound as the maximum of scales determined by the numbers of classes of size at least [MATH]. The lower bound holds for a uniformly random function of that type, and a matching algorithm succeeds on every such function. No intermediate class size is required to occur, and every feasible output alphabet is allowed. The characterization connects the abundant-collision regime associated with set equality to the sparse-target regime of [MATH]-distinctness. In particular, finding the unique [MATH]-collision in type [MATH] has complexity [MATH], where [MATH], resolving an open problem of Belovs. For the lower bound, we introduce a filtered compressed permutation oracle that projects onto a harmonic database subspace after each complete function query. Its [MATH] comparison error over [MATH] queries overcomes the square-root limitation of the unfiltered process. Hidden capacity extensions and moment estimates retain the populations at each intermediate collision order. Matching upper bounds use sampled collision lists and colored adaptive learning graphs, with a coherent decision-to-search conversion that avoids logarithmic overhead. We also give an alternative nested quantum-walk algorithm for three-collision search, matching the bound up to polylogarithmic factors.
tldr: The paper determines tight bounded-error quantum query complexity for finding collisions in functions with prescribed equality-class types, resolving an open problem of Belovs.
motivation: Collision finding is a fundamental quantum query problem, but tight bounds for arbitrary prescribed class-size distributions were not known. The work aims to unify abundant-collision and sparse-target regimes.
method: It introduces a filtered compressed permutation oracle for the lower bound, with hidden capacity extensions and moment estimates, and matching upper bounds via sampled collision lists, colored adaptive learning graphs, and a coherent decision-to-search conversion.
result: For every fixed maximum class size and collision order, the complexity is characterized as the maximum of scales determined by numbers of classes of size at least certain thresholds. In particular, the unique k-collision case has complexity resolving Belovs' open problem.
conclusion: The characterization connects set equality and k-distinctness regimes and provides tight quantum query bounds for collision finding over arbitrary bounded types.

title: Four-Sector Propagation-Trapping Decomposition And Inverse Design Of Initial States In Grover-Coined Quantum Walks On Multiedge Path Graphs
authors: Hamza Bougroura
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Controlling propagation and trapping through initial-state preparation requires an explicit relation between the initial amplitudes and the corresponding directional probabilities. We establish this relation for a discrete-time Grover-coined quantum walk on a multiedge path graph with even degree d = 2M, where M is at least 2, and two equal directional blocks. Each block of an arbitrary local state is expressed as its mean component plus a zero-sum deviation. The Grover coin performs a pure exchange of the two block means and reverses the sign of each zero-sum deviation. Together with the graph routing, this gives a unique orthogonal decomposition into four sectors: propagation in opposite directions and bounded trapping on either side of the launch vertex. We derive the four sector probabilities and solve the inverse problem, constructing initial states for any prescribed nonnegative probability quadruple that sums to unity. Explicit representatives are given for d = 4 and d = 6. Sector-resolved simulations reproduce the predicted motion, conservation of sector weights, and local probability additivity, including repeated spatial overlaps. We also derive the local Grover action for an arbitrary partition into blocks of possibly unequal sizes, explicitly describing how their means are redistributed while each zero-sum deviation remains within its block and changes sign. The framework provides direct control of propagation and trapping within one fixed graph and walk operator through the preparation of the initial state.
tldr: The paper develops an orthogonal four-sector decomposition for Grover-coined discrete-time quantum walks on multiedge path graphs and solves an inverse problem for designing initial states with prescribed propagation/trapping probabilities.
motivation: The work aims to control propagation and trapping in quantum walks through initial-state preparation by explicitly relating initial amplitudes to directional probabilities on a fixed graph and walk operator.
method: It decomposes local states into block means plus zero-sum deviations, analyzes the Grover coin action, and derives sector probabilities for propagation in opposite directions and bounded trapping on either side of the launch vertex; it then constructs initial states for arbitrary nonnegative probability quadruples.
result: The authors obtain explicit sector probabilities, solve the inverse design problem, provide representatives for d=4 and d=6, and confirm sector-resolved dynamics, conservation of sector weights, and local probability additivity via simulations.
conclusion: The framework enables direct control of propagation and trapping within one fixed graph and walk operator through initial-state preparation, with a generalized local Grover action for arbitrary block partitions.

title: Information-Theoretic Threshold Designated-Verifier Digital Signatures For Resource-Constrained Devices
authors: Andrew Wright, Aydin Abadi, Ittoop Vergheese Puthoor
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital signatures are synonymous with data integrity and authenticity. Among applications such as e-commerce, software distribution, and instruction processing they play a vital role in the secure communication of data. Within this context and in preparation for quantum adversarial tactics we present three new information-theoretic threshold designated verifier digital signature schemes and prove them secure against adversary under the standard security criterion. The [MATH]-of-[MATH] multi-signature, [MATH]-of-[MATH] threshold with dealer, and [MATH]-of-[MATH] threshold without dealer designated verifier signature schemes can be implemented with simple mathematical constructs and we demonstrate the efficiency of these with evaluation of signature computation ([MATH] 80\,ms) and verification times ([MATH] 150\,ms) on the resource constrained platform of Raspberry Pi 4. We find our scheme also has equivalent or improved (2[MATH]) performance than a comparable state-of-the-art post-quantum threshold digital signature scheme on both resource constrained devices and the more capable consumer-grade 2025 M5 MacBook Pro.
tldr: Introduces three information-theoretic threshold designated-verifier signature schemes and benchmarks them on resource-constrained devices.
motivation: Digital signatures require security against quantum adversaries and practical efficiency on constrained hardware.
method: Constructs multi-signature, threshold-with-dealer, and threshold-without-dealer designated-verifier schemes using simple mathematical primitives, proves security under a standard criterion, and implements them on a Raspberry Pi 4.
result: Signature computation takes about 80 ms and verification about 150 ms, with equivalent or improved performance versus a comparable post-quantum threshold signature scheme on constrained and consumer hardware.
conclusion: The schemes provide efficient information-theoretic post-quantum signature alternatives for resource-limited settings.

title: 1.56 THz Full-Field Rydberg-Atom Imaging With 0.3 Mm-scale Spatial Response
authors: Xianzhe Li, Yibin Huang, Zhiwen Chen, Kaiqing Zhang, Haixiao Deng
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17558v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: THz imaging via Rydberg-atom up-conversion offers a powerful full-field modality with high sensitivity and rapid acquisition. However sub-millimeter imaging above 1 THz is still constrained by source power and beam-delivery loss. In this paper, we demonstrate a \(50~ \times 50~\) full-field imaging at 1.56~THz by implementing the \(11P_{3/2} \rightarrow 10D_{5/2}\) transition of a cesium Rydberg-atom vapor. The measured spatial response FWHMs are \(0.314~\) in horizontal and \(0.354~\) in vertical for a \(0.5~\) pinhole, alongside a sensitivity of \(31.7~\,^{-1/2}/(6.5 \times 6.5)~\mu^{2}\), and a frame rate up to \(300~\). Under matched illumination, relay, and image-processing conditions, mask imaging at 1.56 THz reproduces finer features and edges with substantially higher edge contrast, deeper intensity-trough separation in line profiles, and recovered detail that remains blurred or unresolved at 0.55 THz. Furthermore, preliminary imaging of a \(200~\mu\) tissue slice suggests morphological correspondence with H\&E histology histology, offered as a proof-of-concept for label-free tissue characterization. By validating the wavelength-dependent resolution scaling in Rydberg THz imaging, this work establishes frequency scaling as a general design principle for sub-millimeter Rydberg-THz imaging.
tldr: The paper demonstrates full-field 1.56 THz imaging using a cesium Rydberg-atom vapor transition, achieving sub-millimeter spatial response and fast frame rates.
motivation: Rydberg-atom THz imaging offers high sensitivity and rapid acquisition, but sub-millimeter imaging above 1 THz is limited by source power and beam-delivery loss.
method: The authors use the 11P3/2 → 10D5/2 transition in cesium Rydberg atoms to perform 50 × 50 full-field imaging at 1.56 THz, characterizing spatial resolution, sensitivity, and frame rate, and compare mask imaging with 0.55 THz results.
result: They measure spatial response FWHMs of 0.314 mm horizontally and 0.354 mm vertically for a 0.5 mm pinhole, a sensitivity of 31.7 μT^-1/2/(6.5 × 6.5) μm², and frame rates up to 300 Hz; tissue-slice imaging shows preliminary morphological correspondence with H&E histology.
conclusion: The work validates wavelength-dependent resolution scaling in Rydberg THz imaging and establishes frequency scaling as a design principle for sub-millimeter Rydberg-THz imaging.

title: Data Re-uploading In Quantum Reservoir Computing
authors: Saud \v{c}indrak, Kaito Kobayashi, Lara Giebeler, Kathy L\"udge
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data re-uploading enhances the learnable function space of parameterized quantum circuits and has become standard practice in circuit-based . Its role in quantum reservoir computing, however, remains largely unexplored. Here, we introduce data re-uploading into physical quantum reservoir computing and show that repeated input encoding significantly enhances the learnability of higher-order nonlinear polynomials and improves performance on chaotic time-series prediction tasks. We consider protocols with either fixed or increasing computational cost and compare them with a complementary dissipative protocol to distinguish the effects of repeated input encoding from those of additional state overwriting. Using the information processing capacity framework, we identify a memory--nonlinearity trade-off: increasing the number of encodings shifts capacity toward higher-order nonlinearities. In contrast, the dissipative protocol does not extend the range of learnable nonlinear orders and yields only limited improvements in task performance. These results establish data re-uploading as an effective means of tuning and enhancing nonlinear processing in physical quantum reservoir computing.
tldr: The paper introduces data re-uploading into physical quantum reservoir computing and shows it enhances learnability of higher-order nonlinear functions and chaotic time-series prediction.
motivation: Data re-uploading is standard in circuit-based quantum machine learning, but its role in quantum reservoir computing remains largely unexplored.
method: The authors incorporate repeated input encoding into physical quantum reservoir computing protocols with fixed or increasing computational cost, comparing them against a dissipative protocol and analyzing performance via the information processing capacity framework.
result: Data re-uploading significantly improves learnability of higher-order nonlinear polynomials and chaotic time-series prediction, revealing a memory-nonlinearity trade-off as more encodings shift capacity toward higher-order nonlinearities; the dissipative protocol yields only limited gains.
conclusion: Data re-uploading is an effective tuning mechanism for enhancing nonlinear processing in physical quantum reservoir computing.

title: Dissipation-induced Integrability In A Spin-1 Chain And A Bose-Hubbard Mixture
authors: Kaixiang Lu, Mingdi Xu, Xiang-Ping Jiang, Lei Pan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct a nonintegrable spin-1 chain that acquires a Yang--Baxter integrable no-jump Hamiltonian through a single dissipative channel per bond. Energy is the only nontrivial finite-range charge of the isolated periodic bulk. Interference cancels the reverse spin conversions, leaving directed moves that obey nil-Coxeter relations and generate commuting charges of increasing range on the open chain. We obtain the full Liouvillian spectrum at any chain length and identify an exponentially large set of blocked spin configurations whose superpositions are all stationary. Resolving the bond outputs leaves the no-jump Hamiltonian unchanged; each bond on which two configurations differ then contributes equally to their dephasing. In a two-component Bose--Hubbard chain, opposite loss phases produce counterpropagating species whose motion and collisions enter a common transfer matrix when interspecies attraction matches intraspecies repulsion. At this coupling, redistributing a pair costs no interaction energy in the atomic limit. Such bond interference offers a route to integrability in other open quantum many-body systems.
tldr: The paper constructs dissipative spin-1 and Bose-Hubbard chain models in which bond-local dissipation induces an integrable no-jump Hamiltonian and allows exact Liouvillian analysis.
motivation: The authors aim to show how a nonintegrable many-body system can acquire integrability through carefully engineered dissipation rather than coherent tuning.
method: They use a single dissipative channel per bond to cancel reverse spin conversions, obtain a Yang-Baxter integrable no-jump Hamiltonian obeying nil-Coxeter relations, and solve the full Liouvillian spectrum; they also analyze a two-component Bose-Hubbard chain via a common transfer matrix.
result: They obtain the full Liouvillian spectrum at arbitrary chain length, identify exponentially many stationary superpositions of blocked spin configurations, and show that bond-resolved dephasing contributions are equal for configurations differing on a bond; in the Bose-Hubbard mixture, counterpropagating species enter a common transfer matrix at matched couplings.
conclusion: Bond interference provides a general route to dissipation-induced integrability in open quantum many-body systems, with potential extensions beyond the specific spin-1 and Bose-Hubbard examples.

title: Efficient Representations By Peps: Critical Free-fermion And Chiral Topological States
authors: Rahul Trivedi Ignacio Cirac
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct projected entangled-pair state (PEPS) approximations to various many-body states in 2D lattices with global error at most [MATH] and bond dimension polynomial in the system size and [MATH]. They include critical free-fermion models in two dimensions, as well as chiral topological states. For the two-dimensional nearest-neighbor tight-binding model at half filling, our construction combines Gaussian wavelet transformations with matrix product state approximations of the one-dimensional chains, as well as selected fermionic swap operations. For arbitrary uniformly gapped, finite-range quadratic Hamiltonians, we give a different construction based on repeated one-particle filtering, which yields Gaussian PEPS in any spatial dimension. Those include, for instance, [MATH] models or a Chern-insulator in a square lattice, for which we give an explicit construction. Finally, we prove that Gutzwiller projections of a fixed number of identical Gaussian PEPS approximations to free-fermion states at arbitrary filling do not amplify considerably the approximation error. This provides a polynomial-bond PEPS approximations to the resulting states, including familiar lattice chiral-spin-liquid states.
tldr: Constructs efficient PEPS representations with polynomial bond dimension for critical 2D free-fermion models and chiral topological states, including Gutzwiller-projected chiral spin liquids.
motivation: Tensor-network representations of gapless and topologically ordered 2D states are notoriously expensive; the authors ask whether free-fermion structure can be exploited to obtain provably efficient PEPS approximations.
method: Combines Gaussian wavelet transformations with MPS approximations of 1D chains plus fermionic swap gates for the half-filled tight-binding model, and introduces a repeated one-particle filtering construction yielding Gaussian PEPS for uniformly gapped finite-range quadratic Hamiltonians in any dimension; Gutzwiller projections are analyzed for error amplification.
result: Global error at most epsilon is achieved with bond dimension polynomial in system size and 1/epsilon, covering critical free-fermion models, Chern insulators, and Gutzwiller-projected chiral spin liquids.
conclusion: Free-fermion and chiral topological states admit provably efficient PEPS descriptions, extending tensor-network representability results to gapless and topologically non-trivial 2D systems.

title: Toward The Minimal Set Of Information Inequalities In Regenerating Codes: An Algebraic Approach
authors: Rui-Juan Jing, Laigang Guo, Yan-Feng Xie, Chun-Ming Yuan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Information-theoretic outer bounds for exact-repair regenerating codes can be formulated as linear programs, but the associated Shannon-type systems contain many implicit equalities and redundant inequalities. We directly specify a reduced system for the [MATH] exact-repair model using the closure structure induced by its repair dependencies. Nonempty closed sets index the reduced joint-entropy coordinates, and inseparable edges determine the defining inequalities. We prove equivalence with the initial system by characterizing its implicit equalities and establishing sufficient redundancy criteria. We also give an algorithm that constructs the directly defined system for any [MATH], count its entropy coordinates, and derive an explicitly computable upper bound on its number of inequalities. For every [MATH], we prove that the reduced system has no implicit equalities and that each distinct defining inequality is nonredundant and defines a facet in the nonempty closed-set coordinate space. Exact enumerations for [MATH] verify the reported system sizes.
tldr: The paper constructs a reduced system of Shannon-type information inequalities for exact-repair regenerating codes using an algebraic closure approach.
motivation: Information-theoretic outer bounds for exact-repair regenerating codes are linear programs, but their Shannon-type systems contain many implicit equalities and redundant inequalities, motivating a minimal directly defined system.
method: The authors use repair-dependency closure structures to index joint-entropy coordinates by nonempty closed sets, define inequalities from inseparable edges, prove equivalence with the initial system, and provide an algorithm for constructing and counting the reduced system.
result: They show the reduced system has no implicit equalities, each defining inequality is nonredundant and facet-defining in the closed-set coordinate space, and give an explicitly computable upper bound on the number of inequalities, with exact enumerations verifying system sizes.
conclusion: This provides a minimal algebraic characterization of information inequalities for exact-repair regenerating codes, but it is a classical coding/information-theory result without direct quantum information relevance.

title: New Results On The Subfield Metric
authors: Ana Kosovac, Jeanette Plechinger, Nikola Spirovski, Violetta Weger
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we further develop the theory of the recently introduced [MATH]-subfield metric. We investigate extremal codes, classical bounds and asymptotic densities in this setting. We first study codes attaining a Singleton-type bound, called Maximum [MATH]-subfield Distance (M[MATH]D) codes. We establish structural restrictions on their parameters and extend the theory to sublinear codes. We then investigate the asymptotic density of M[MATH]D codes in several parameter regimes and compare their behavior with that of MDS and MRD codes. We then turn to a Plotkin-like bound, where we construct a family of constant-weight codes attaining the bound and classify all non-degenerate linear constant-weight codes for [MATH]. Finally, we complement the collection of classical coding-theoretic bounds available for the [MATH]-subfield metric by deriving Griesmer-, Elias- and Johnson-type bounds.
tldr: The paper develops the theory of the recently introduced ℓ-subfield metric for codes over subfields, establishing extremal codes, classical bounds, and asymptotic densities.
motivation: The subfield metric, a recently introduced alternative distance measure for codes, lacked a systematic coding-theoretic treatment of extremal/optimal codes and classical bounds analogous to those available for the Hamming and rank metrics.
method: The authors study Maximum ℓ-subfield Distance (MℓD) codes, derive structural restrictions on their parameters, extend results to sublinear codes, analyze asymptotic densities of MℓD codes, and derive Plotkin-, Griesmer-, Elias-, and Johnson-type bounds, constructing constant-weight codes that meet the Plotkin-like bound.
result: Structural parameter restrictions for MℓD codes are established, asymptotic densities are compared with MDS and MRD codes across parameter regimes, and all non-degenerate linear constant-weight codes are classified for the scalar case; new bounds complement the existing collection.
conclusion: The work provides a fairly complete classical coding-theoretic framework (extremal codes, densities, bounds) for the subfield metric, which may later serve as a tool for code-based cryptography or quantum code constructions, but it remains a purely classical coding-theory contribution.

title: Hamming And Johnson-Type Bounds For Joint Error Correction And Detection
authors: Raymond W. Yeung Yulin Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive upper bounds on the size of codes for joint error correction and detection over classical [MATH]-ary Hamming spaces. A [MATH] joint error correcting and detecting code corrects every error of weight at most [MATH] and detects every error whose weight lies between [MATH] and [MATH]. We establish equivalent conditions for this decoding requirement using Hamming balls and Hamming rings, and derive a joint bound that reduces to the Hamming bound when [MATH]. We introduce joint perfect codes and show that binary repetition codes attain the joint bound whenever [MATH]. For codes satisfying [MATH], we investigate an alternative joint bound based on ring multiplicity and constant-weight code bounds. A further argument using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and pairwise ring intersections yields a refined joint bound that is always at least as strong as the original joint bound. We then incorporate an additional outer Hamming shell to obtain a Johnson-type extension. This extension provides a strict improvement for binary codes with [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH]. These results connect sphere-packing bounds with the geometry of joint error correction and detection.
tldr: The paper derives Hamming- and Johnson-type sphere-packing upper bounds on the size of classical q-ary codes that jointly correct errors up to weight t and detect errors up to weight s.
motivation: Joint error correction and detection is a practically motivated coding requirement, yet classical bounds had been developed mainly for pure correction or pure detection; the authors aim to unify these into a single sphere-packing framework.
method: They characterize the decoding requirement via Hamming balls and rings, derive a joint bound reducing to the Hamming bound in the pure-correction limit, define joint perfect codes, and refine the bound using ring multiplicities, constant-weight code bounds, Cauchy-Schwarz, and pairwise ring intersections, plus an outer Hamming shell for a Johnson-type extension.
result: Binary repetition codes are shown to attain the joint bound for certain parameters, and the refined and Johnson-type bounds give strict improvements for various binary parameter regimes such as t=1, s=2, and t=2.
conclusion: The work connects classical sphere-packing bounds with the geometry of joint error correction and detection, but remains entirely within classical coding theory with no quantum information-theoretic content.

title: Hardware-aware Sampling And QPU-informed Monte Carlo With Quantum Annealers
authors: Seungyeob Jwa, Jangho Kim, Sunghee Kim, Sunkyu Lee, Weonjong Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17842v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how the physical representation of a logical model affects sampling by quantum annealers and its use in corrected Monte Carlo. The square-lattice Ising model provides controlled classical references. Fixed embeddings with one physical qubit per logical spin reach [MATH] spins. Comparisons with uniform two-qubit chains and mixed chain lengths show that matching mean energy leaves differences in magnetization and correlations. Extended-range conditional predictors improve the description of mixed embeddings, distinguishing their residual correlations from those of the tested uniform embeddings. Independent calibration checks and fixed-scale annealing scans show that temperature shifts alone do not determine distributional agreement. Normalized autoregressive models learned from QPU samples provide proposals with exact Metropolis--Hastings and multiple-try corrections on larger periodic lattices. These preserve the target distribution, although block updates alone relax critical magnetization slowly. Complementary direct-QPU updates reveal how block size and fitted-temperature correction affect acceptance and spin motion. Together, the results support prioritizing one-qubit representations and short uniform chains, while separating hardware sampling fidelity from the convergence of corrected Monte Carlo.
tldr: The paper studies how different physical embeddings of logical Ising spins on a D-Wave-style quantum annealer affect sampling distributions, and uses QPU samples as proposals inside corrected (Metropolis-Hastings / multiple-try) Monte Carlo schemes.
motivation: Quantum annealers are increasingly used as samplers, but it is unclear how the hardware embedding (one qubit per spin vs. chains of qubits) and effective temperature distort the sampled Boltzmann distribution, and whether these samples can be safely corrected to yield unbiased Monte Carlo.
method: Square-lattice Ising models with controlled classical references are embedded in fixed one-qubit-per-spin layouts and uniform/mixed chain layouts up to large spin counts; magnetization, correlations and extended-range conditional predictors are compared, and normalized autoregressive models trained on QPU samples serve as proposals within exact Metropolis-Hastings and multiple-try correction schemes on larger periodic lattices.
result: Matching mean energy does not guarantee matching magnetization or correlations, temperature shifts alone cannot explain distributional disagreement, and the corrected Monte Carlo preserves the target distribution, though block updates alone relax critical magnetization slowly; one-qubit representations and short uniform chains perform best.
conclusion: The authors recommend prioritizing one-qubit embeddings and short uniform chains, and argue that hardware sampling fidelity should be assessed separately from the convergence properties of the corrected Monte Carlo algorithm.

title: Parameterized Weakest-Precondition Calculus For Fine-grained Properties Of Quantum Loops
authors: Tianshi Yu, Minbo Gao, Li Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18132v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum loops may execute arbitrarily many iterations, and understanding their runtime behavior requires knowing how often they terminate, how long terminating runs take, and how common very long runs are. We develop a compositional weakest-precondition framework for analyzing these properties on possibly infinite-dimensional state spaces. It uses parameterized predicates: families of quantum effects indexed by a positive observation scale. These families retain runtime information even when the expected runtime is infinite and can be reused through sequential composition and nested loops. We prove that weakest-precondition equations for loops have unique solutions in the parameterized predicate domain. From the asymptotic behavior of the derived weakest preconditions, we then recover these runtime properties and quantify the influence of very long terminating executions. For the classic discrete-time quantum walk on the one-dimensional infinite line with one absorbing boundary at the origin and the Hadamard gate as its coin operator, we verify its termination probability [MATH], conditional mean [MATH], and logarithmic growth of the conditional capped second moment. We then reuse the walk's specification to verify the termination probability and conditional mean runtime of an outer loop that repeatedly invokes it.
tldr: The paper develops a compositional parameterized weakest-precondition calculus for reasoning about termination probabilities, conditional mean runtime, and tail behavior of quantum loops on infinite-dimensional state spaces, demonstrated on a discrete-time quantum walk with an absorbing boundary.
motivation: Quantum loops can run for an unbounded number of iterations, so understanding their runtime behavior requires tools that characterize how often they terminate, how long terminating runs take, and how heavy the tail of very long runs is — questions not handled well by existing expected-runtime analyses that break down when expectation diverges.
method: The authors introduce parameterized predicates, families of quantum effects indexed by a positive observation scale, and prove that the weakest-precondition equations for loops admit unique solutions in this domain; the semantics support sequential composition and nested loops, and asymptotic analysis of derived preconditions recovers runtime properties.
result: For the Hadamard-coin discrete-time quantum walk on the infinite line with one absorbing boundary, they verify termination probability, conditional mean runtime, and logarithmic growth of the conditional capped second moment, then reuse the walk's specification to verify termination probability and conditional mean runtime of an enclosing loop.
conclusion: The framework provides a reusable compositional proof technique for fine-grained runtime properties of quantum programs, extending weakest-precondition reasoning to settings where expected runtime is infinite.

title: Remarks On Souriau's Geometric Thermodynamics For Weak Two-Dimensional Euler Flows
authors: Jean-Pierre Magnot
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine infinitesimal symmetries of relative entropy on low-regularity vorticity spaces and compare them with symmetries of stationary laws of weak two-dimensional Euler trajectories. Relative-entropy invariance under sample-space transformations is equivalent to preservation of the reference law; the corresponding weak infinitesimal condition is a vanishing reference-divergence identity. White-noise vorticity has an infinite-dimensional family of such symmetries, generated by smooth area-preserving transport. At the level of path laws, however, marginal entropy symmetries need not preserve temporal correlations. We first give a continuous Gaussian counterexample, including its infinitesimal form. We then establish a counterexample directly for stationary white-noise weak Euler path laws: explicit non-isometric area-preserving shears preserve the white-noise marginal but cannot preserve an Euler path law satisfying the standard symmetrized weak vorticity equation. We also examine the reduction of guaranteed entropy symmetries under conditioning by renormalized energy. These observations distinguish thermodynamic symmetry, Hamiltonian covariance, and statistical path dynamics without asserting a selection principle for nonunique weak solutions.
tldr: The paper studies symmetries of relative entropy for low-regularity 2D Euler flows and shows that marginal entropy symmetries need not preserve Euler path-law dynamics.
motivation: It aims to compare geometric thermodynamic symmetries of relative entropy with symmetries of stationary weak 2D Euler trajectory laws.
method: The author analyzes infinitesimal symmetries of relative entropy on vorticity spaces, constructs Gaussian and white-noise counterexamples, and examines conditioning by renormalized energy.
result: Explicit area-preserving shears can preserve the white-noise marginal while failing to preserve an Euler path law satisfying the symmetrized weak vorticity equation.
conclusion: The work distinguishes thermodynamic symmetry, Hamiltonian covariance, and statistical path dynamics without proposing a selection principle for nonunique weak solutions.

title: Foundation Tensor Networks Generalize Across Quantum Lattice Systems
authors: Michael Lindsey Ryan T. Grimm
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural quantum states and tensor networks have emerged as leading techniques for simulating quantum many-body systems. However, disordered systems remain extremely challenging in both frameworks as they require computation of the ground state for every realization of the disorder. Recently, neural quantum states have been used to construct foundation models that generate the ground state directly from the Hamiltonian. Still, they are hindered by the need to perform extensive sampling to estimate observables. To address these difficulties, we introduce the foundation tensor network (FTN), which uses a neural network to generate the tensor network representation of the ground-state wavefunction from the Hamiltonian. To accelerate training, we develop a technique, called , based on iterated one-dimensional belief propagation that reduces the cost of computing the energy expectation value to just two tensor contractions. We use FTNs to calculate the critical parameters of the glass transition in the quantum Edwards-Anderson model via finite-size scaling analysis. To facilitate rapid averaging, we use a moment-generating function to evaluate the order parameter, lowering the cost to a single tensor contraction. We obtain high-fidelity estimates for the critical parameters by averaging over 500,000 disorder realizations.
tldr: The paper introduces foundation tensor networks, which use a neural network to generate tensor-network ground-state wavefunctions across disordered quantum lattice Hamiltonians.
motivation: Simulating disordered quantum many-body systems is costly because ground states must be computed for each disorder realization, and neural quantum states still require extensive sampling for observables.
method: The authors train a neural network to output tensor-network representations from Hamiltonians and accelerate energy evaluation using iterated one-dimensional belief propagation, reducing it to two tensor contractions.
result: They apply the approach to the quantum Edwards-Anderson model, estimate glass-transition critical parameters via finite-size scaling, and average over 500,000 disorder realizations using a moment-generating function for the order parameter.
conclusion: Foundation tensor networks provide an efficient generative tensor-network framework for disordered quantum lattice systems, but the work is primarily a computational many-body method rather than a contribution aligned with the listed quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid-systems directions.

title: Learning And Generating Time Trajectories Of Multidimensional Stochastic Processes
authors: Zihan Xu, Changho Kim, Andy J. Nonaka, Yuanran Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a multidimensional statistics-informed neural network (SINN) framework for learning and generating trajectories of multicomponent stochastic processes. SINN is built upon a deterministic recurrent neural network that takes streams of white-noise sequences as input and generates ensembles of stochastic trajectories whose statistical properties match those of the underlying stochastic dynamics. While SINN has been demonstrated for various one-dimensional non-Markovian processes, extending it to multidimensional processes is essential for real-world applications. Here, we present key developments toward this goal. First, because direct estimation of multivariate probability density functions (PDFs) becomes computationally challenging with increasing dimension, we represent joint-distribution information using collections of one-dimensional PDFs constructed from linear combinations of the process components. Second, to accommodate the larger set of statistical objectives required to characterize multidimensional processes, we adopt a self-adaptive loss-balancing strategy that dynamically weights the components of the total loss function. Third, we introduce a reference-normalized validation framework that interprets statistical discrepancies relative to the finite-sample variability between independent target ensembles. We also investigate the role of the input white-noise dimension in SINN performance. We evaluate the proposed approach using a Langevin benchmark based on two coupled Duffing oscillators and further demonstrate its applicability to the Langevin dynamics of the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam chain and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations of a lattice Lotka-Volterra model. Our results demonstrate that the multidimensional SINN framework provides a practical approach for modeling multidimensional stochastic dynamics.
tldr: A statistics-informed neural network (SINN) framework is extended to learn and generate trajectories of multidimensional stochastic processes using white-noise-driven recurrent networks.
motivation: SINN was previously limited to one-dimensional non-Markovian processes; real-world applications require multidimensional stochastic dynamics, which introduces challenges in estimating multivariate PDFs, balancing many statistical objectives, and validating results with finite samples.
method: Joint-distribution information is encoded via collections of one-dimensional PDFs of linear combinations of process components, combined with a self-adaptive loss-balancing strategy and a reference-normalized validation framework based on finite-sample variability between target ensembles.
result: The framework is validated on a Langevin benchmark of two coupled Duffing oscillators, the Langevin dynamics of the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam chain, and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations of a lattice Lotka-Volterra model, showing the role of input noise dimension in performance.
conclusion: The multidimensional SINN framework offers a practical data-driven approach for modeling and sampling complex stochastic dynamics, though it is a classical computational/ML contribution with no quantum information or quantum thermodynamic content.

title: Optimal Heterogeneous Diffusivity Profiles For Mean First-passage Minimization
authors: Luiz Menon
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate how spatially varying diffusivity can be optimized to minimize the mean first-passage time for escape from a spherical shell with an inner reflecting boundary and an outer absorbing boundary. Under a fixed volume-averaged diffusivity, we derive a variational condition for arbitrary spatial dimension and stochastic integration prescription. For particles starting at the inner boundary, we obtain exact optimal profiles in one dimension, with homogeneous diffusion being optimal under the Stratonovich prescription. In higher dimensions, the optimal Stratonovich profile becomes decreasing. The optimal It\^o profile is decreasing in all dimensions, whereas the optimal H\"anggi--Klimontovich profile is increasing in one and two dimensions and can exhibit a maximum in dimensions greater than two. For particles starting beyond the inner boundary, optimal profiles can exhibit a discontinuity at the initial position, with constant diffusivity in the inner region. Numerical optimization complements these results, showing how geometry, stochastic prescription, and initial position jointly determine the diffusivity distribution that minimizes the mean escape time.
tldr: The paper derives optimal spatially varying diffusivity profiles that minimize mean first-passage time for escape from a spherical shell under fixed volume-averaged diffusivity.
motivation: The authors aim to understand how inhomogeneous diffusion can be optimized to accelerate first-passage processes in bounded geometries, accounting for different stochastic integration prescriptions.
method: They use variational calculus to derive a general optimality condition for arbitrary dimension and stochastic prescription, complemented by exact solutions in one dimension and numerical optimization in higher dimensions.
result: For particles starting at the inner boundary, the optimal Stratonovich profile is homogeneous in 1D and decreasing in higher dimensions; the Itô profile is always decreasing, while the Hänggi–Klimontovich profile is increasing in 1D and 2D and can have a maximum above 2D. Discontinuous optimal profiles arise when starting away from the inner boundary.
conclusion: Optimal diffusivity landscapes depend jointly on geometry, stochastic prescription, and initial position, providing design principles for controlling mean escape times in diffusion-limited systems.

title: Optically-induced Electric Aharonov-Bohm Effect
authors: Gabriel P. Martins, Herman Batelaan, Pablo L. Saldanha
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although it was proposed almost 70 years ago, the electric version of the Aharonov-Bohm (AB) effect, where the interference pattern of quantum charged particles is affected by electric fields that do not interact locally with them, was never experimentally implemented. Here we propose a feasible way to experimentally verify such an important effect, for an electron double-slit interferometer with the slits carved in a nonlinear crystal. The AB phase is generated by a quasi-DC electric field induced in the crystal with the passage of a light pulse (the optical rectification effect) while the electron is superposed in the two slits. We show that this procedure can change the interference pattern of a ensemble of electrons even if they are subjected to negligible electric fields during their propagation, considering feasible parameters.
tldr: The paper proposes an experimentally feasible scheme to observe the electric Aharonov-Bohm effect using an electron double-slit interferometer carved into a nonlinear crystal, where a light pulse induces a quasi-DC electric field via optical rectification.
motivation: The electric version of the Aharonov-Bohm effect, predicted nearly 70 years ago, has never been experimentally demonstrated, despite its foundational importance for understanding electromagnetic potentials in quantum mechanics.
method: An electron double-slit interferometer is fabricated in a nonlinear crystal. A light pulse generates a quasi-DC electric field inside the crystal through optical rectification while the electron is in a superposition of the two slits, producing an Aharonov-Bohm phase shift.
result: The authors show that feasible parameters allow the induced electric field to modify the electron interference pattern even though the electrons experience negligible local electric fields during propagation.
conclusion: This proposal provides a practical route to experimentally verify the electric Aharonov-Bohm effect and could stimulate further foundational tests of gauge potentials in quantum mechanics.

title: Recursive Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz
authors: Stuart Flannigan Lennart Binkowski
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17537v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The recursive quantum approximate optimisation algorithm~(RQAOA) shrinks an unconstrained combinatorial optimisation problem by eliminating one variable at a time, guided by correlations measured in variational quantum states. We extend this recursion to constrained problems by building on the quantum alternating operator ansatz, which restricts the evolution to feasible solutions through a feasible initial state and feasibility-preserving mixers. However, every elimination alters the feasibility structure, so that such a mixer for the original problem generally fails to be one for the subproblems. Previous extensions to Maximum Independent Set and Minimum Vertex Cover sidestep this with tailored reduction rules that keep every subproblem within the original problem class. We resolve this by identifying, for a given constraint structure, a broader problem class that is closed under all eliminations, and by efficiently constructing feasible initial states and feasibility-preserving mixers for every class member. We do so for monotone constraints, such as for the knapsack problem, for linear equality constraints with polynomially bounded weights, including Hamming weight constraints, and for combinations of equality constraints with a single inequality constraint, such as the cardinality-constrained knapsack problem. Conversely, we show that these restrictions cannot be lifted in general without leaving the realm of efficient constructions. Exact simulations on knapsack and vertex-weighted max-bisection instances demonstrate that our recursive scheme can outperform both its non-recursive counterpart and penalty-based QAOA and RQAOA.
tldr: The paper extends recursive QAOA to constrained combinatorial optimization by constructing feasible initial states and feasibility-preserving mixers for recursively reduced subproblems.
motivation: RQAOA eliminates variables one at a time but its constrained version struggles because elimination changes the feasibility structure, so mixers valid for the original problem may fail on subproblems.
method: The authors identify constraint classes closed under eliminations, including monotone constraints, polynomially bounded linear equalities, Hamming-weight constraints, and equality constraints with one inequality, and efficiently construct feasible initial states and mixers for every class member.
result: Exact simulations on knapsack and vertex-weighted max-bisection instances show the recursive constrained scheme can outperform non-recursive QAOA, penalty-based QAOA, and RQAOA.
conclusion: Recursive quantum alternating operator ansatz provides an efficient framework for constrained optimization under certain constraint structures, though the constructions cannot be generalized arbitrarily.

title: Antihelical Edge States In Photonic Metacrystals
authors: Ke-Yi Zeng, Zi-Xuan Gao, Zhou Zhou, Xiao-Dong Chen, Jian-Wen Dong
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Antihelical edge states represent a gapless form of boundary transport in which modes with opposite spin counterpropagate along a given boundary, while modes sharing the same spin propagate in the same direction on opposite boundaries. Here we show that such states arise naturally within a modified Kane-Mele framework realized in an electromagnetic-dual photonic metacrystal with staggered bianisotropy. Reversing the spin-dependent next-nearest-neighbor coupling on one sublattice reorganizes the bulk spectrum into a spin-polarized Dirac semimetal characterized by spin-dependent energy shifts of the Dirac cones rather than a bulk gap. This bulk reorganization generates tilted edge-mode dispersions in zigzag ribbons and gives rise to antihelical edge transport coexisting with bulk states. Full-wave simulations confirm the corresponding bulk and edge behaviors. Extending the analysis to finite geometries, simulations further reveal discrete corner-localized modes. A realistic design based on split-ring metaatoms is proposed to realize the required staggered bianisotropy and spin-dependent energy shifts of the Dirac cones. Furthermore, we show that the tensorial freedom of the bianisotropic constitutive relations enables continuous manipulation of the electromagnetic pseudospin basis while preserving the antihelical boundary transport. These results provide a practical route for engineering unconventional gapless boundary transport in photonic Dirac systems.
tldr: The paper proposes and simulates antihelical edge states in a bianisotropic photonic metacrystal based on a modified Kane-Mele model.
motivation: The authors aim to realize unconventional gapless boundary transport where opposite-spin modes counterpropagate on a given edge while same-spin modes propagate in the same direction on opposite edges.
method: They modify the Kane-Mele framework using staggered bianisotropy in an electromagnetic-dual photonic metacrystal and perform full-wave simulations of bulk, edge, and finite-geometry corner modes.
result: The modified bulk spectrum becomes a spin-polarized Dirac semimetal with spin-dependent Dirac-cone shifts, producing tilted zigzag edge dispersions and antihelical edge transport coexisting with bulk states.
conclusion: The work provides a practical photonic platform for engineering antihelical gapless boundary transport and continuously manipulating the electromagnetic pseudospin basis via bianisotropic constitutive relations.

title: Rigidity For Pivotal Braided R-categories Of Moderate Growth And Applications To Vertex Operator Algebras
authors: Robert Mcrae
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be an abelian pivotal braided r-category with simple unit object [MATH] over any field. We present a ChatGPT-generated proof, prompted by Bin Gui, that any object [MATH] in [MATH] of moderate growth, in the sense that [MATH] for some [MATH], where [MATH] is the Grothendieck-Verdier duality functor of [MATH]. Using this variant, we show that if [MATH] is a simple self-contragredient vertex operator algebra such that the category [MATH] of [MATH]-cofinite grading-restricted generalized [MATH]-modules is closed under contragredient modules, then [MATH] is a locally finite [MATH]-linear abelian rigid braided ribbon category. We also show that if [MATH] is a simple [MATH]-graded self-contragredient [MATH]-cofinite vertex operator algebra, then the category of all grading-restricted generalized [MATH]-modules is a (not necessarily semisimple) modular tensor category.
