Simulations in geometric and 3GPP TR 38.901 UMi-NLOS channels reveal that authentication performance is governed by available spatial degrees of freedom, channel correlation, and operating signal-to-noise ratio. The proposed equilibrium strategies effectively balance communication rate and security, outperforming conventional benchmark policies.
tldr: The paper analyzes RIS-assisted physical-layer authentication as a Bayesian game under partial channel knowledge and characterizes equilibrium strategies balancing communication rate and security.
motivation: Physical-layer authentication can be strengthened by a reconfigurable intelligent surface, but attack-defense interactions under incomplete channel information require a game-theoretic treatment.
method: The authors formulate a finite-action Bayesian game in which each agent observes only its own channel, derive Bayesian Nash equilibrium strategies, and evaluate them in geometric and 3GPP channel models.
result: Simulations show that authentication performance depends on spatial degrees of freedom, channel correlation, and SNR, and the proposed equilibrium strategies outperform conventional benchmarks.
conclusion: Game-theoretic RIS-assisted authentication under partial channel knowledge can effectively balance communication rate and security.

title: Hello Again: Exploiting Replay Protected Monotonic Counters To Brute-Force Windows Hello PINs
authors: Christian Werling, Matti Finder, Hans Niklas Jacob, Julian Prein, Niclas K\"uhnapfel, Jean-Pierre Seifert
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18126v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Windows Hello is the primary authentication mechanism on over one billion Windows 11 devices, supporting PINs as short as four digits. Such low-entropy PINs are viable only because the TPM's anti-hammering protection mitigates brute-force attacks. Most modern x86 platforms rely on firmware TPMs (fTPMs) that persist their non-volatile (NV) state, including the lockout state, to SPI flash. On newer platforms, rollback prevention of this state is delegated to the flash chip via Replay Protected Monotonic Counters (RPMCs), a JEDEC-standardized mechanism operating over a physically accessible bus. We present the first practical security analysis of RPMC in shipping x86 systems. Using low-cost interposer hardware, we identify multiple implementation flaws, two of which fundamentally undermine RPMC's security model: First, Winbond SPI flash - the leading NOR flash vendor with over 25% market share - leaks its HMAC key under voltage glitching, enabling arbitrary counter forgery. Second, AMD's NV controller does not verify RPMC increments, so an interposer can suppress them unnoticed. Moreover, AMD platforms without RPMC flash appear to lack NV rollback protection altogether: on two AMD desktops, reflashing an old image resets the fTPM's lockout counters. Both flaws enable rollbacks of the fTPM's NV state (AMD, Intel, or Pluton), including its lockout counters. We demonstrate this end-to-end on locked, encrypted hardware: our setup finds a 4-digit Windows Hello PIN in 40 hours instead of 69 days. A compromised PIN also grants access to device-bound keys and Hello-based enterprise SSO. The same primitive defeats BitLocker's TPM+PIN pre-boot protector, reducing the worst-case time for a default-length 6-digit PIN from 19 years to 20 days.
tldr: A hardware security analysis showing that Replay Protected Monotonic Counters in x86 SPI flash can be subverted to roll back firmware TPM lockout counters, enabling brute-force of Windows Hello PINs and BitLocker pre-boot authentication.
motivation: Windows Hello relies on TPM anti-hammering to make low-entropy PINs safe, but on modern x86 platforms rollback protection of the fTPM non-volatile state is delegated to the flash chip via RPMC, a mechanism never practically audited in shipping systems.
method: The authors use low-cost SPI interposer hardware to intercept and manipulate the bus, perform voltage glitching on a Winbond NOR flash to extract its HMAC key, and test whether AMD's NV controller verifies RPMC increments, plus reflash old firmware images on RPMC-less AMD desktops.
result: They find two fundamental flaws (HMAC key leakage under voltage glitching enabling counter forgery, and unverified RPMC increments on AMD), demonstrate end-to-end rollback of lockout counters on locked encrypted hardware, cracking a 4-digit PIN in 40 hours instead of 69 days and reducing BitLocker 6-digit PIN worst case from 19 years to 20 days.
conclusion: RPMC-based rollback protection in current x86 platforms is insecure, undermining TPM anti-hammering and thus the security of Windows Hello PINs, BitLocker TPM+PIN, device-bound keys and enterprise SSO.

title: Safety Analysis Of Parameterized Networks With Shared Counters
authors: Arnaud Sangnier June Roupin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study networks with an unbounded number of processes sharing some natural counters that can be decremented, incremented and tested to zero. We look at two safety problems: the first one asks whether there is a network with an execution bringing a process in a given final state and the other one asks the execution to bring all the processes in the final state. In their full generality, these two problems are undecidable, but we show that decidability can be regained by either using a single counter or by forbidding the use of zero-tests (as it is is the case in Vector Addition Systems with States). For these decidable cases, we obtain low complexity results, the problems being solvable either in non-deterministic logarithmic space or in polynomial time.
tldr: The paper studies decidability and complexity of safety verification problems for parameterized networks of processes that communicate via shared natural-valued counters.
motivation: Parameterized distributed systems with shared counters generalize Vector Addition Systems with States, and their safety verification is undecidable in full generality, so identifying decidable fragments is desirable.
method: The authors consider two safety problems over unbounded process networks with counters supporting increment, decrement, and zero-test, and restrict either to a single counter or to counter systems without zero-tests.
result: Both safety problems are shown decidable in the restricted cases, solvable in non-deterministic logarithmic space or in polynomial time, whereas the general formulations are undecidable.
conclusion: Tight restrictions on counter usage restore decidability with low complexity, delineating the boundary between decidable and undecidable safety verification for such networks.

title: Why Finite Intelligence Works In An Infinite World: A Mathematical Theory
authors: Mojtaba Soltanalian
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An information system often has to learn before it knows what it will be asked. A finite representation can succeed without recording an infinite environment in full when those asks share collective structure, rather than demand unrelated facts scattered arbitrarily across it. We formalize this phenomenon through future-task information, the minimum retained information needed to preserve decision value relative to the available evidence. A joint decision-regret state records posterior comparisons among actions for every permitted task. Under compactness assumptions, every retained representation admits a calibrated replacement based on this state, preserving all task regrets without increasing information; the resulting information-regret curve equals an operational coding rate. Two exact boundaries govern finite preservation: weak-star closure for a fixed action count, and the singular mass of the source-evidence law when all finite action menus are admitted. Collective structure determines information requirements beyond individual-question difficulty. Families with identical source laws, pairwise task metrics, and individual-task rates can have different high-resolution exponents. Covariance-identical coordinate and parity families have different exact rate-distortion curves, with optimal parity retention characterized by a sharp Fourier-entropy inequality. For balanced nested task families, refinement sizes and weighted reach determine the rate within an additive constant, attained by prefix coding under explicit decay conditions. Nonlinear learning and computational separations distinguish preservation from efficient discovery and use. The proposed mathematical theory identifies which shared decision requirements allow finite information to remain useful for infinitely many possible purposes.
tldr: The paper develops a mathematical theory of when finite information representations suffice for infinitely many future decision tasks, using decision-regret states, coding rates, and rate-distortion boundaries.
motivation: An information system must often learn before knowing future tasks, so the authors ask when finite retained information can preserve decision value across an infinite environment rather than recording it fully.
method: They formalize future-task information via joint decision-regret states and calibrated representations, then characterize preservation limits through weak-star closure, singular source-evidence mass, coding rates, and Fourier-entropy inequalities.
result: They identify exact boundaries for finite preservation, show collective task structure can determine information requirements beyond individual-task difficulty, and derive distinct rate-distortion curves for covariance-identical coordinate and parity families.
conclusion: The theory clarifies which shared decision requirements allow finite information to remain useful for infinitely many purposes, distinguishing preservation from efficient discovery and use.

title: Consensus-Based Optimization Of Path-Integral Free Energy For Model Predictive Control
authors: Daisuke Inoue, Yuyang Huang, Dante Kalise
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose CBO-MPPI, a sampling-based predictive controller that applies consensus-based optimization (CBO) to the free energy underlying model predictive path integral control (MPPI). Under hard constraints, this objective rewards sampling neighborhoods containing feasible, low-cost trajectories under perturbation. Standard MPPI performs a local stochastic search by updating one nominal control sequence from Gaussian perturbations around it. In CBO-MPPI, we estimate the free energy at multiple nominal centers from local rollouts. These estimates define a shared consensus that guides drift and diffusion, and the final selected center supplies an MPPI weighted-mean output. For the associated mean-field model, we establish well-posedness and, under additional assumptions, convergence toward a free-energy minimizer. In simulations of obstacle navigation, pendulum swing-up, and planar-arm manipulation under equal rollout budgets, at high temperatures, CBO-MPPI attains lower free energy than MPPI and multi-start MPPI and maintains greater obstacle clearance than CBO-MPC.
tldr: CBO-MPPI combines consensus-based optimization with model predictive path-integral control, estimating the path-integral free energy at multiple nominal centers to improve sampling-based trajectory optimization under hard constraints.
motivation: Standard MPPI performs only a local stochastic search around a single nominal control sequence, which can be inefficient or unsafe when constraints and high temperatures make the free-energy landscape multimodal.
method: The authors estimate free energy at several nominal centers from local rollouts, use these estimates to define a shared consensus that drives drift and diffusion of the sampling distribution, and output an MPPI weighted mean from the selected center; they also analyze well-posedness and convergence of the associated mean-field model.
result: In obstacle navigation, pendulum swing-up, and planar-arm manipulation under equal rollout budgets, CBO-MPPI attains lower free energy than MPPI and multi-start MPPI at high temperatures and maintains greater obstacle clearance than CBO-MPC.
conclusion: Consensus-based optimization offers a principled way to globalize the free-energy minimization in path-integral control, though the benefits are most pronounced at high sampling temperatures.

title: Resurgence Without The Borel Plane: Mellin-Barnes Summation And Analytic Stokes Reconstruction
authors: Roberto Ricci
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a route to resurgence without the Borel plane: sums of divergent perturbative series and their encoded nonperturbative monodromy are constructed directly in complex perturbative order. In the Analytic Umbral Framework (AUF), an analytic coefficient clock produces the sum through a Mellin-Barnes integral and its monodromy through a bare inverse Mellin transform. Neither a Borel transform nor continuation of a Borel germ is required for this construction. For Watson-admissible Gevrey clocks, the completion agrees with the canonical Borel-Laplace sum in the guaranteed directions. When the admissible aperture exceeds [MATH], the clockwise difference of adjacent logarithmic determinations is given by [MATH] times the inverse-Mellin carrier. This carrier is also the AUF completion of a null clock and is flat on the overlap. The sum and its aggregate monodromy are thus obtained ''in one shot'', before resolving individual actions and fluctuation series. Euler's equation, zero-dimensional quartic models, the scaled Gamma function and a solvable [MATH] toy model exemplify the procedure, and show how further analysis recovers directional Stokes variations. The lognormal benchmark extends the construction beyond every finite Gevrey order: no finite-order Borel transform gives a convergent germ, yet explicit clock-selection conditions yield an AUF completion and a nonzero ordinary flat carrier. Distributed relaxation supplies a physical realization of this growth class. AUF therefore both reconstructs familiar resurgent information without Borel-plane continuation and extends completion beyond finite-order Borel-Laplace summation.
tldr: The paper develops a Mellin-Barnes and analytic-coefficient approach to resurgence that avoids Borel-plane continuation, reconstructing divergent series and their nonperturbative monodromy directly in complex perturbative order.
motivation: Resurgence theory conventionally relies on Borel transforms and Borel-Laplace summation, which can be restrictive, especially beyond finite Gevrey order; the author aims for a Borel-plane-free construction.
method: Within the Analytic Umbral Framework, an analytic coefficient clock produces sums via Mellin-Barnes integrals and monodromy via inverse Mellin transforms, with comparisons to canonical Borel-Laplace summation for Watson-admissible Gevrey clocks.
result: The construction recovers familiar resurgent information in one shot before resolving individual actions and fluctuation series, matches Borel-Laplace sums in guaranteed directions, and extends completion beyond finite-order Borel summation, illustrated by Euler's equation, quartic models, Gamma function, and a lognormal benchmark.
conclusion: AUF reconstructs standard resurgent data without Borel-plane continuation and generalizes completion to growth classes inaccessible to finite-order Borel-Laplace summation.

title: Polynomial Integrals And Poisson Structures Of The Pais-Uhlenbeck Oscillator
authors: Gulmammad Mammadov Ilmar Gahramanov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We classify the autonomous polynomial integrals of the nondegenerate fourth-order Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator. For a rational frequency ratio [MATH] in lowest terms, the two sector energies together with the real and imaginary parts of a single ladder product generate all polynomial integrals, subject to one defining relation. The smallest total degree of an integral not expressible through the sector energies is [MATH], and this bound is attained. For an irrational ratio only polynomials in the sector energies are conserved. In normal-mode variables the commensurate case is the negative oscillator resonance, and the classification realizes its invariant theory in the original higher-derivative variables. Two compatible Poisson structures generate the same dynamics with an indefinite and a positive-definite Hamiltonian. They induce different brackets on the same physical generators. We show that diagonal rescalings of the generators identifying the two abstract Poisson algebras exist only when [MATH] or [MATH] is even, and that none of them preserves the physical domain of nonnegative sector energies. Finally, we express the generators in terms of the original coordinate and its first three derivatives. The classical multiplier identity gives their variational characteristics in closed form and shows that the additional resonant integrals cannot arise from point variational symmetries.
tldr: The paper classifies polynomial integrals and Poisson structures of the nondegenerate fourth-order Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, including commensurate and incommensurate frequency cases.
motivation: The Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator is a higher-derivative mechanical model whose integrability and Poisson structure are of mathematical and theoretical interest, but the work is not aimed at quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors analyze autonomous polynomial integrals, sector energies, ladder products, normal-mode variables, compatible Poisson structures, and variational characteristics via the classical multiplier identity.
result: They show that for rational frequency ratios all polynomial integrals are generated by sector energies and a ladder product subject to one relation, with a minimal total degree bound; for irrational ratios only sector-energy polynomials are conserved. They also show that rescalings identifying the two Poisson algebras exist only under parity conditions and never preserve the physical nonnegative-energy domain.
conclusion: The classification clarifies the invariant theory and Poisson geometry of the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator and shows that additional resonant integrals cannot arise from point variational symmetries.

title: Uncertainty Evaluation Of Length Measurement By Spectral Domain Interferometry With super-Gaussian Windowing
authors: Dae Hee Kim, Yoonkwon On, Sunghoon Eom, Chu-Shik Kang, Yoon-Soo Jang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this study, we evaluate the measurement uncertainty of spectral domain interferometry with super-Gaussian windowing, which has significant potential for interferometer-based dimensional calibration services owing to its simple configuration and nanometer-level precision. A super-luminescent diode (SLD) with a broadband spectrum was used as the light source for high-precision length measurement, and a frequency-calibrated spectrometer captured the spectral interference signal. The length measurement results were compared with a laser displacement interferometer. To evaluate the measurement uncertainty, numerical simulations were performed by considering the intensity-noise level of the CCD in the spectrometer and the frequency-axis uncertainty of the spectrometer. Through a comprehensive uncertainty analysis supported by numerical simulations, the combined standard uncertainty of the measured length was evaluated as sqrt((10 nm)^2 + (9.7x10^(-6)xL)^2). The resulting uncertainty budget provides a metrological basis for extending SLD-based SDI with super-Gaussian windowing toward interferometric dimensional calibration tasks over the millimeter-scale range.
tldr: This paper evaluates measurement uncertainty in spectral-domain interferometry with super-Gaussian windowing for nanometer-precision length measurement and dimensional calibration.
motivation: Spectral-domain interferometry with super-Gaussian windowing is attractive for interferometer-based dimensional calibration due to its simple setup and nanometer-level precision, but its uncertainty budget requires careful characterization.
method: The authors use a broadband superluminescent diode source and a frequency-calibrated spectrometer to capture spectral interference signals, compare length measurements with a laser displacement interferometer, and perform numerical simulations accounting for CCD intensity noise and frequency-axis uncertainty.
result: The combined standard uncertainty is evaluated as sqrt((10 nm)^2 + (9.7e-6 × L)^2), providing a metrological uncertainty budget over the millimeter-scale range.
conclusion: The uncertainty analysis supports the use of SLD-based spectral-domain interferometry with super-Gaussian windowing for interferometric dimensional calibration tasks.

title: Cartan Dynamics And Limit Sets On Flag Manifolds
authors: \'angel Cano, Marlon M. L\'opez-Flores, Jos\'e Seade, Andrew Shaw
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17510v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The classical convergence principle describes the collapse of the Riemann sphere under divergent sequences of M\"obius transformations. We develop its counterpart for arbitrary real semisimple Lie groups acting on flag manifolds, and use it to study limit sets and domains of discontinuity of discrete subgroups. The key is to let the source move: the destination of [MATH] under [MATH] is the set of all limits of [MATH] with [MATH]. Our destination formula computes it as the closure of a unipotent orbit, determined by the Cartan data and a bounded Levi factor. The stratified convergence principle organises these destinations into families of translated Schubert varieties attached to boundary points of a compactification of the group. Over the complex numbers, the destination relation is the support of Brion's limiting graphs in the wonderful compactification, providing scheme structures, multidegrees and diagonal intersections. For discrete groups, the union of destination relations determines proper discontinuity and whether a largest domain exists. It relates Quint's flag limit set, Conze--Guivarc'h, Kulkarni and Myrberg sets to the recurrent set, while balanced choices of cells yield domains for every discrete subgroup, without Anosov hypotheses. For symmetric-power actions of non-elementary Kleinian groups on [MATH], we compute the largest domain by a multiplicity bound at points of the classical limit set; for [MATH] it strictly contains the Kulkarni domain, which equals the equicontinuity region. We also obtain nonempty largest domains for Zariski-dense cusped Hitchin groups with unipotent elements, and examples of strongly irreducible groups with no largest domain.
tldr: The paper develops a 'stratified convergence principle' for arbitrary real semisimple Lie groups acting on flag manifolds, generalizing the classical Möbius convergence principle on the Riemann sphere, and applies it to limit sets and domains of discontinuity of discrete subgroups.
motivation: The classical convergence principle for Möbius transformations on the Riemann sphere lacks a general counterpart for higher-rank semisimple Lie groups and flag manifolds, which is needed to characterize limit sets and discontinuity domains of discrete subgroups beyond Anosov settings.
method: The authors let the source point vary, computing the destination of a divergent group element as the closure of a unipotent orbit determined by Cartan data and a bounded Levi factor, organizing these into translated Schubert varieties and, over the complex numbers, linking them to Brion's limiting graphs in the wonderful compactification.
result: Destination relations recover and relate Quint's flag limit set, Conze–Guivarc'h, Kulkarni and Myrberg sets to the recurrent set, yield domains of discontinuity for every discrete subgroup without Anosov hypotheses, and give explicit largest domains for symmetric-power actions of Kleinian groups, including cases strictly containing the Kulkarni domain.
conclusion: The framework unifies and extends several classical notions of limit sets and domains of discontinuity for discrete group actions on flag manifolds through Cartan data and Schubert-variety geometry.

title: Agent-written Heuristics Versus Commercial Solvers On Unsolved Job-shop Benchmark Instances
authors: Andre Albrecht, Enzo Morosini Frazzon, Leandro C. Coelho, Bruno Vieira
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Commercial solvers are the standard tool for difficult scheduling problems. We study whether a frontier large language model, used as a coding agent with open-source tools only, can match them in quality and speed. We report every run, and independent checkers verify every schedule. On the 100,000-operation job shop tai_100_1000_1, an agent-written solver reached 525,515, below OptalCP, Hexaly, and CP Optimizer. Unchanged, it improved all ten instances of the family and closed two. With equal budgets on the same workstation, it ended 0.0-1.8% above the lower bound, against 2.6-5.8% for CP Optimizer and 2.4-4.4% for Hexaly. On the Behnke-Geiger flexible job shops, an agent-written tabu search improved 11 of 32 open instances. With two transport robots, an agent-written solver improved seven of ten MKT instances. New lower bounds show that four published MKT values cannot be attained on the distributed instance files. Agent-run improvement campaigns closed eight further instances.
tldr: The paper evaluates whether a frontier LLM coding agent using open-source tools can match commercial solvers on difficult job-shop scheduling benchmarks.
motivation: Commercial solvers are standard for hard scheduling problems, and the authors ask whether agent-written heuristics can compete in solution quality and speed.
method: An LLM agent writes solvers/heuristics that are run on large job-shop and flexible job-shop benchmark instances, with independent checkers verifying schedules and comparisons against OptalCP, Hexaly, and CP Optimizer.
result: Agent-written solvers improved many open instances, closed several benchmarks, and achieved lower gaps to lower bounds than commercial solvers under equal budgets on some instances.
conclusion: LLM coding agents with open-source tools can produce competitive scheduling heuristics for certain hard benchmark instances, though the work is outside quantum information research.

title: Compatible By Construction: Bottom-Up Nonlinear Model Reduction Without Interface Bases
authors: Youngsoo Choi Youngkyu Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonlinear manifolds can provide compact representations of solutions to partial differential equations (PDEs), but generating training data and learning these representations on large domains remain costly. We present a bottom-up framework that reuses local nonlinear representations learned on a small training domain to solve larger PDE systems. A shared nonlinear decoder represents the full set of degrees of freedom owned by each subdomain, without separate interior and interface models. Each global degree of freedom has a unique owner, and local residuals directly use decoded state values from the corresponding neighboring subdomains. The resulting discrete state is single-valued by construction, eliminating the need for independent interface copies and additional interface compatibility constraints. Physical coupling is retained through the original time-discrete PDE residual. With the decoder held fixed, the subdomain-specific reduced coordinates are determined jointly by minimizing this residual, and the Gauss--Newton system is assembled from local contributions. Experiments on parameterized viscous Burgers and incompressible Navier--Stokes problems demonstrate reuse on larger domains without retraining. Comparisons with local proper orthogonal decomposition models under the same coupling construction show favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-offs in the tested regimes.
tldr: A bottom-up nonlinear model-reduction framework that reuses locally learned decoders to solve larger PDE systems without interface bases or retraining.
motivation: Learning nonlinear solution manifolds for PDEs on large domains is costly because training data generation and representation learning scale poorly with domain size.
method: Local nonlinear decoders learned on a small subdomain are shared across subdomains, with each global degree of freedom having a unique owner; subdomain reduced coordinates are obtained jointly by minimizing the original time-discrete PDE residual via Gauss-Newton assembled from local contributions.
result: Experiments on parameterized viscous Burgers and incompressible Navier-Stokes problems show reuse on larger domains without retraining, with favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs versus local POD models under the same coupling construction.
conclusion: Single-valued, compatibility-free reduced states by construction enable scalable nonlinear reduced-order modeling across subdomains, avoiding interface bases and separate interface constraints.

title: Wireless Node Ranking Via Fourier-Driven Maximum-Likelihood Estimation (extended Version)
authors: Hannes Frey Daniel Schneider
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17973v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We apply non-abelian Fourier theory to the problem of maximum-likelihood estimation of the order of a line topology, based on signal strength measurements under shadowing only. This yields up to a 60-fold speedup over standard methods for uncorrelated shadowing. Moreover, for correlated Gaussian shadowing with a singular covariance (e.g. the joint path-loss model), maximum-likelihood recovery is exact and independent of the shadowing variance (an infinite Le Cam threshold), which our implementation confirms for [MATH] as high as 7.0. The key object is the covariance's null space. Its dimension is fixed by the topology; its orientation depends on the correlation function only through the per-link variances. Although the mechanism formally requires an exact line, it is robust to small perturbations of the formation: an approximate kernel recovers as well as the exact one. We explore the dependence on the perturbation in detail for five nodes.
tldr: The paper applies non-abelian Fourier theory to maximum-likelihood estimation of node ordering in a wireless line topology from shadowed signal-strength measurements.
motivation: Recovering the order of nodes along a line from noisy received-signal-strength data is a classical wireless-localization problem where naive maximum-likelihood search is computationally expensive.
method: Non-abelian Fourier (representation-theoretic) techniques are used to accelerate the maximum-likelihood search over permutations, exploiting the null space of the shadowing covariance matrix, with analysis for correlated Gaussian shadowing including singular covariances such as the joint path-loss model.
result: The approach yields up to a 60-fold speedup for uncorrelated shadowing and exact, variance-independent recovery (infinite Le Cam threshold) for correlated singular-covariance shadowing, confirmed numerically up to a correlation magnitude of 7.0, with robustness to small perturbations of the linear formation.
conclusion: The method provides an efficient and statistically sharp solution to classical wireless node-ordering, but it lies entirely outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: Movable Antenna-Aided Isac: A Time- And Frequency-Division Framework
authors: Yuyan Zhou, Haocheng Hua, Jie Xu, Rui Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates movable-antenna (MA)-enhanced integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) under time division duplex (TDD) and frequency division duplex (FDD) protocols, where sensing and communications occupy orthogonal time and frequency resources, respectively. A wideband target-position Cram\'er-Rao bound (CRB) is derived under a pulse-radar framework with pulse compression, incorporating delay and angle estimation error bounds in Cartesian coordinates. Both bounds depend on sensing power; the delay bound also depends on sensing bandwidth, while the angle bound depends on the effective aperture determined by the antenna position vector (APV). A worst-case position CRB over a prescribed target region ensures robust sensing performance. For multiuser downlink communication, joint APV and resource-allocation problems are formulated for TDD and FDD to maximize the minimum achievable user rate subject to the sensing requirement. An alternating optimization algorithm is developed for FDD, while TDD is addressed by searching over feasible sensing pulse numbers combined with APV optimization. Representative scenarios clarify how MA improves channel orthogonality and enlarges the sensing aperture, and how these effects shape the TDD/FDD rate comparison. Numerical results show that APV optimization enlarges the communication-sensing tradeoff region over fixed-position antenna benchmarks. The optimized configurations exhibit distinct tendencies: TDD favors a larger antenna position variance, whereas FDD favors better channel orthogonality among users.
tldr: This paper develops a time- and frequency-division framework for movable-antenna (MA)-enhanced integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), optimizing antenna position vectors and resource allocation to balance wideband sensing CRB and multiuser downlink rate.
motivation: Movable antennas offer a new degree of freedom for shaping wireless channels and sensing apertures, but their joint use for sensing and communication under TDD/FDD duplexing has not been systematically characterized.
method: The authors derive wideband position Cramér-Rao bounds (delay and angle) under a pulse-radar framework with pulse compression, then formulate joint APV and resource-allocation problems maximizing the minimum user rate under sensing constraints, solved by alternating optimization (FDD) and pulse-number search with APV optimization (TDD).
result: APV optimization enlarges the communication-sensing tradeoff region relative to fixed-position antenna benchmarks, with TDD favoring larger antenna position variance and FDD favoring better inter-user channel orthogonality.
conclusion: Movable antennas provide a practical design lever for ISAC in both duplexing modes, though the appropriate antenna geometry depends strongly on whether time- or frequency-division is used.

title: Beyond Attack-Based Accuracy: Rethinking Adversarial Robustness Evaluation Through Structural Gradient Alignment
authors: Hanrui Wang, Yu Luo, Shuo Wang, Xingbo Dong, Zhe Jin, Isao Echizen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Visual adversarial robustness remains a fundamental security property as vision systems evolve from conventional classifiers to vision-language models (VLMs) and large vision-language models (LVLMs), with visual inputs remaining an attack surface across generations. Yet existing evaluation methods often depend on prescribed attacks, in-distribution data, extensive probing, or classifier-specific formulations, limiting external auditing of diverse models. We introduce Structural Gradient Alignment (SGA), a complementary robustness metric measuring the structural alignment between input content and objective-conditioned local model sensitivity. SGA uses a few randomly sampled, unlabeled public probes that need not follow the downstream task distribution and only one input-gradient computation per model--probe pair. Across 38 distinct DNNs, VLMs, and LVLMs, SGA produces rankings consistent with attack-based references. Without robustness references, uncalibrated SGA achieves [MATH] average pairwise agreement across eight public-probe conditions, outperforming the strongest overall baseline in all eight by [MATH] percentage points on average. With known robustness orders of anchor models, calibrated SGA increases agreement to [MATH]. These results demonstrate an attack-agnostic, computationally efficient robustness signal across conventional DNNs, VLMs, and autoregressive LVLMs, downstream tasks, threat norms, probe distributions, and evaluator-knowledge settings. Our implementation is available at [URL].
tldr: The paper proposes Structural Gradient Alignment (SGA), an attack-agnostic robustness metric for vision models based on the alignment between input content and objective-conditioned input gradients.
motivation: Existing adversarial robustness evaluations rely on prescribed attacks, in-distribution probes, or classifier-specific formulations, which hinders external auditing of diverse and evolving vision systems including VLMs and LVLMs.
method: SGA estimates robustness by measuring structural alignment between input content and local model sensitivity, using a few unlabeled random public probes and a single input-gradient computation per model-probe pair, with optional calibration against anchor models.
result: Across 38 DNNs, VLMs, and LVLMs, SGA rankings agree with attack-based references, and uncalibrated SGA achieved the best average pairwise agreement across eight public-probe conditions, improving further with calibration.
conclusion: SGA provides a computationally efficient, attack-agnostic robustness signal spanning architectures, tasks, threat norms, and probe distributions, offering a practical tool for external auditing of visual model robustness.

title: Online Allocation With Differential Privacy
authors: Jianyi Yang, Xingyu Zhou, Mostafa Mushsharat, Shaolei Ren
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study private online allocation problems, where allocation decisions must satisfy differential privacy (DP) to protect sensitive user information while optimizing performance under limited resources. We first formalize differential privacy notions suited to different privacy requirements in online allocation and establish the fundamental performance limits of any algorithm under these definitions. Based on these insights, we propose PPOA, a privacy-preserving meta algorithm for online allocation, and establish sufficient conditions under which PPOA preserves Joint DP (JDP) or Local DP (LDP) while achieving asymptotically near-optimal performance. Building on these conditions, PPOA can be instantiated into a variety of concrete algorithms. In particular, we present the specific designs, which include PPOA-DMD that preserves JDP and LDP and PPOA-FTRL that preserves JDP. We analyze their performance under both adversarial and stochastic settings and characterize the fundamental trade-offs between DP and allocation performance. Finally, we demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed algorithms via numerical experiments on AI model routing in battery-powered edge systems.
tldr: The paper formalizes differential privacy notions for online allocation problems, derives fundamental performance limits, and proposes a meta-algorithm (PPOA) with instantiations achieving near-optimal performance under joint or local DP.
motivation: Online allocation systems (e.g., ad delivery, model routing) rely on sensitive user data, so allocation decisions must be made privately while still optimizing resource-constrained performance.
method: The authors define DP notions tailored to online allocation, prove lower bounds on achievable performance, and introduce PPOA, a privacy-preserving meta-algorithm with sufficient conditions for preserving JDP/LDP, instantiated as PPOA-DMD and PPOA-FTRL.
result: PPOA-based algorithms attain asymptotically near-optimal competitive ratios under both adversarial and stochastic inputs while preserving JDP or LDP, and numerical experiments on battery-aware AI model routing show superior performance.
conclusion: The work characterizes the fundamental trade-off between differential privacy and online allocation performance, providing a general framework for private online decision-making.

title: Tractable Importance Sampling For Monte Carlo Privacy Accounting
authors: Arun Ganesh Galen Andrew
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluating tight Differential Privacy (DP) parameters for DP matrix factorization with privacy amplification by sampling requires analyzing high-dimensional, correlated Gaussian mixtures. Because integrating these mixture distributions to find the exact privacy failure probability ([MATH]) is analytically intractable, these mechanisms are typically analyzed using Monte Carlo accounting. However, standard sampling suffers from prohibitive variance when estimating small [MATH] associated with strict privacy guarantees, which in turn requires a large sample complexity, making Monte Carlo accounting inefficient. We demonstrate that Monte Carlo accounting can be made much more efficient via importance sampling. We give a shifted importance sampling proposal distribution parameterized by a stretch factor [MATH]. We prove a closed-form bound [MATH] on the support of the importance-weighted estimator that holds identically for both directions of the hockey-stick divergence, show that [MATH] is log-convex so that the optimal [MATH] is a one-dimensional root-finding problem, and show that the resulting estimator seamlessly plugs into the KL-Hoeffding verification protocol used by past work, with a sample complexity reduced by exactly a factor of [MATH].
tldr: The paper develops importance sampling techniques to make Monte Carlo privacy accounting for differentially private matrix factorization more sample-efficient.
motivation: Tight differential privacy accounting for mechanisms with privacy amplification by sampling requires estimating small failure probabilities of high-dimensional correlated Gaussian mixtures, where standard Monte Carlo sampling has prohibitive variance.
method: The authors introduce a shifted importance sampling proposal parameterized by a stretch factor, prove a closed-form bound on the importance-weighted estimator for both directions of the hockey-stick divergence, and show log-convexity so that the optimal stretch factor is found by one-dimensional root-finding.
result: The resulting estimator integrates with the KL-Hoeffding verification protocol and reduces sample complexity by an exact factor, making Monte Carlo privacy accounting substantially more efficient.
conclusion: Importance sampling provides a tractable and provably better approach to tight privacy accounting for DP matrix factorization with sampling amplification.

title: Binarization As An Attack Surface In Weightless Neural Networks
authors: Lucas Senos Coutinho, Matheus Vargas, Pedro Teixeira, Heudson Tosta Mirandola, Ori Rottenstreich, Priscila Machado Vieira Lima, Leandro Santiago, Daniel Sadoc Menasche
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17646v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weightless Neural Networks (WNNs) are lightweight classifiers that binarize their inputs and learn by storing binary patterns in lookup memories, which makes them attractive for resource-constrained tasks such as intrusion detection. Because a small perturbation that crosses no binarization threshold leaves the binary input unchanged, WNNs may appear naturally robust to adversarial examples; a perturbation that does cross a threshold, however, can still change the prediction. We study this tension in WiSARD, the canonical RAM-based WNN, and in two variants that replace its memories with Bloom filters, Bloom WiSARD and BTHOWeN. A continuous perturbation reaches these classifiers only by crossing an encoding threshold, changing at least one binary tuple, and redirecting a memory query; we formalize this mechanism with a threshold-crossing bound and a response-margin certificate for standard Boolean WiSARD. Controlled MNIST experiments compare linear and data-driven thermometer encodings under model-agnostic sensitivity probes, a score-based Simulated Annealing attack, and surrogate-transfer attacks. Changing only the encoding while keeping each model otherwise fixed shows that encoding granularity can trade a small clean-accuracy loss for a large decrease in attack success. On the Bot-IoT, CICIDS, and UNSW-NB15 intrusion-detection datasets, adversarial perturbations lead WNN detectors to classify many attacks as normal traffic and to raise false alarms, even when their aggregate accuracy remains high.
tldr: This paper studies how binarization in weightless neural networks creates an adversarial attack surface, especially for intrusion-detection classifiers.
motivation: Weightless neural networks appear robust because small perturbations may not cross binarization thresholds, but threshold-crossing perturbations can still alter predictions.
method: The authors formalize threshold-crossing and response-margin effects in WiSARD and Bloom-filter variants, then evaluate thermometer encodings under sensitivity probes, simulated annealing attacks, and surrogate-transfer attacks on MNIST and intrusion-detection datasets.
result: Encoding granularity can trade a small clean-accuracy loss for a large reduction in attack success, while adversarial perturbations can cause WNN detectors to misclassify attacks as normal traffic and raise false alarms.
conclusion: Binarization is a meaningful attack surface in weightless neural networks, and encoding choices materially affect adversarial robustness in security-critical classification tasks.

title: LLMs Are Vulnerable To Malicious Requests With Indistinguishable Intent
authors: Wenzhuo Xu, Zonghao Ying, Deyue Zhang, Dongdong Yang, Xiangzheng Zhang, Quanchen Zou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Jailbreak attacks can circumvent the safety mechanisms of Large Language Models (LLMs) and lead to the generation of harmful or policy-violating content. We first examine eight jailbreak methods against an LLM-based filter and observe that requests resembling normal user queries tend to have higher filter pass rates than those containing obvious anomalous patterns. This observation motivates the hypothesis that resemblance to normal requests may contribute to jailbreak success. We introduce , a framework that uses an auxiliary LLM to construct detailed requests and interacts with the victim model in a single turn. Across 11 victim models and three datasets, the complete DGA pipeline achieves high attack success rates under our automated judging criterion, including rates above 95\% in several evaluated settings. We also evaluate a DGA-aware filter and conduct a user study on everyday requests with ambiguous or dual-use intent. The survey documents differing expectations about whether models should respond; the usability costs of the filter remain to be measured.
tldr: The paper introduces DGA, an auxiliary-LLM framework that crafts detailed, natural-looking single-turn requests to jailbreak 11 victim LLMs, achieving attack success rates above 95% in several settings.
motivation: The authors observe that jailbreak prompts resembling ordinary user queries pass LLM-based safety filters more often than obviously anomalous ones, suggesting that intent indistinguishability drives attack success.
method: They first benchmark eight jailbreak methods against an LLM-based filter, then build DGA, which uses an auxiliary LLM to generate detailed naturalistic requests and queries the victim model in a single turn across three datasets and 11 models; they also test a DGA-aware filter and run a user study on dual-use requests.
result: The full DGA pipeline attains high attack success under an automated judge, exceeding 95% in multiple configurations; the user survey reveals divergent expectations about whether models should answer ambiguous everyday requests.
conclusion: Resemblance to benign queries is a key vulnerability of LLM safety filtering, and the usability costs of intent-based defenses remain unquantified.

title: Securing Multi-Agent Systems By Design
authors: Xilong Wang, Xiaoxing Chen, Neil Gong
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent systems solve complex tasks by decomposing them into subtasks, delegating the subtasks to agents, and aggregating the agents' responses using an aggregation rule. Malicious agents can manipulate the final solution by providing malicious responses to their assigned subtasks. In this paper, we first propose response manipulation attacks (ReMA), which iteratively optimize malicious responses to maximize attack effectiveness. Specifically, we formulate untargeted and targeted attacks as optimization problems and develop an approach to approximately solve these problems by iteratively refining malicious responses based on feedback from a surrogate multi-agent system. To defend against such attacks, we further propose SecMAS, a secure aggregation rule that leverages the semantic similarities among agent responses to select the response that is most consistent with a sufficiently large subset of the other responses. We theoretically establish security guarantees for SecMAS against both untargeted and targeted attacks. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that existing aggregation rules are vulnerable to ReMA, whereas SecMAS effectively defends against all evaluated attacks, including adaptive variants of ReMA, while maintaining utility comparable to that of existing aggregation rules.
tldr: The paper introduces response manipulation attacks (ReMA) against multi-agent LLM systems and proposes SecMAS, a semantics-based secure aggregation rule with theoretical security guarantees.
motivation: Multi-agent systems that decompose tasks and aggregate agent responses are vulnerable to malicious agents injecting manipulated responses, and existing aggregation rules offer no robustness.
method: Untargeted and targeted attacks are cast as optimization problems and approximately solved by iteratively refining malicious responses using feedback from a surrogate multi-agent system; the defense SecMAS selects the response most semantically consistent with a sufficiently large subset of others.
result: Existing aggregation rules are empirically vulnerable to ReMA, while SecMAS defends against all evaluated attacks, including adaptive variants, with security guarantees and utility comparable to baseline aggregation rules.
conclusion: Secure-by-design aggregation can harden multi-agent LLM pipelines against response manipulation without sacrificing task performance.

title: On Structure-Aware Sat Solving
authors: Eugene Goldberg
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although modern SAT solvers have made remarkable progress, they still exploit formula structure only to a limited extent. We present two techniques that make SAT solving more structure-aware and provide experimental results showing their promise. The first technique ``[MATH]'' the formula by reducing interaction between its parts. This is achieved by adding new variables, using existential quantifiers, and applying a procedure called partial quantifier elimination. The second technique exploits the notion of a [MATH] [MATH]. The latter establishes that a formula is unsatisfiable by proving that certain literals of its clauses are redundant. We show that using local proofs makes SAT solving more formula-specific.
tldr: The paper presents two structure-aware techniques for improving SAT solving by reducing variable interaction and using local proofs of literal redundancy.
motivation: Modern SAT solvers exploit formula structure only to a limited extent, leaving room for algorithmic improvements.
method: The first technique transforms formulas by adding variables, using existential quantifiers, and applying partial quantifier elimination; the second exploits local proofs that establish unsatisfiability via redundant literals.
result: Experimental results indicate that both techniques show promise for making SAT solving more formula-specific and structure-aware.
conclusion: The work suggests that structure-aware SAT techniques can enhance solver performance, though it is purely classical and unrelated to quantum information science.

title: The Qbf Gallery 2026
authors: Cynthia Peyrer, Luca Pulina, Martina Seidl
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The QBF Gallery 2026 is the latest evaluation event of (dependency) quantified Boolean formula (QBF) solving technology. Its goal is to assess the current state-of-the-art, enable the evaluation of novel solvers on newly curated benchmark instances and present the progress made since the previous competition. This report discusses the solvers, instances and tools submitted by the community and introduces new benchmark collections for evaluation. We evaluate solvers in three tracks, reflecting most common input formats in (dependency) QBF solving. In addition to those main evaluations, we investigate effects of preprocessing and include a track of new crafted benchmark families. The results are analyzed using various metrics and complementary statistics on solver similarities, different memory limitations and performance across formula families. Finally, the dedicated benchmarks for each track are made available as an artifact to support future research and reproducible evaluation.
tldr: This report presents the QBF Gallery 2026, an evaluation event benchmarking state-of-the-art solvers for (dependency) quantified Boolean formulae across three tracks.
motivation: The QBF community needs a recurring, reproducible evaluation to track progress in quantified Boolean formula solving and to expose novel solvers to newly curated benchmark instances.
method: Community-submitted solvers, instances and tools are evaluated in three tracks reflecting common (dependency) QBF input formats, plus a crafted-benchmark track, with additional analysis of preprocessing effects, solver similarity, memory limits and per-family performance.
result: The evaluation ranks solvers per track, quantifies the impact of preprocessing, and reports complementary statistics on solver behaviour and resource-limited performance across benchmark families.
conclusion: All track benchmarks are released as an artifact to support reproducible future research and continued progress in QBF solving technology.

title: PrivacyPR: A Dataset Of Real-World Privacy Fixes For Benchmarking Privacy-Aware Code Review
authors: Hua Yang, Aditya Bhardwaj, Shidong Pan, Bowen Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents increasingly review code, yet whether they catch the privacy defects that laws such as the GDPR require software to avoid remains largely untested, partly because few datasets connect real privacy defects to their accepted fixes and review context. We present PrivacyPR, a dataset of 4,131 merged GitHub pull requests (PRs) from 1,469 repositories, created between June 2018 and January 2024. Each PR includes its commits, diffs, review discussion, and LLM-generated labels for privacy relevance, fix type, and GDPR principles. PrivacyPR provides 1,169 high-confidence privacy fixes and 1,643 non-fix PRs, together with Verified, a manually checked split of 250 privacy fixes and 250 non-fix PRs, and Small, a 100 + 100 subset for evaluation. On Verified, both annotators endorsed 72% of the LLM's GDPR-principle assignments. Beyond supporting empirical study of how privacy defects arise and are fixed, PrivacyPR provides a benchmark for privacy-aware code review on real, developer-accepted fixes. Its evaluation harness reverts each fix to reintroduce the defect. On Small, two coding agents detect only 42-51% of defects under a generic review prompt, but 88-91% when explicitly asked to check privacy, while flagging 11-15% of non-fix PRs. These results show that privacy defects can be detected by coding agents, but that detection depends strongly on review intent and comes with false alarms. Data, code, reviews, judge verdicts, and an extensible evaluation harness are publicly available at [URL].
tldr: PrivacyPR is a dataset of 4,131 merged GitHub pull requests annotated with LLM-generated privacy-relevance, fix-type, and GDPR-principle labels, intended as a benchmark for privacy-aware code review by coding agents.
motivation: Coding agents increasingly review code, but it is largely untested whether they detect privacy defects required by regulations such as the GDPR, partly due to the lack of datasets linking real privacy defects to accepted fixes and review context.
method: The authors curate PRs from 1,469 repositories (2018-2024) with commits, diffs, and review discussions; they add LLM-generated labels, manually verified splits (Verified: 250 fixes + 250 non-fixes; Small: 100 + 100), and an evaluation harness that reverts each fix to reintroduce the defect.
result: Annotators endorsed 72% of the LLM's GDPR-principle assignments; on the Small split, two coding agents detect only 42-51% of defects under a generic prompt but 88-91% when explicitly asked to check privacy, while flagging 11-15% of non-fix PRs.
conclusion: Privacy defects are detectable by coding agents, but detection depends strongly on review intent and comes with false alarms; the dataset and harness are publicly released to support further study.

title: CANTraj: Recovering Vehicle Trajectories From Can Signals In Naturalistic Driving
authors: Yuhang Wang, Jingxin Yang, Chuheng Wei, Suyang Chen, Haozhuang Chi, Hao Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open driving releases and usage-based insurance programs often claim to prevent privacy breaches by omitting GPS records when sharing or collecting vehicle data. However, removing GPS coordinates from driving logs does not erase the location information carried by vehicle signals. While prior route-inference attacks have demonstrated that speed, steering, and driving events can be matched to road networks to reconstruct trajectories, existing studies rely on inconsistent prior assumptions and evaluation metrics and are tested only on small, restricted datasets, making their results difficult to compare and their real-world effectiveness uncertain. We release CANTraj, a naturalistic driving dataset pairing decoded CAN events with time-aligned GNSS trajectories (3,940 drives, 454 drivers), and CANTraj-Bench for evaluating trajectory recovery (3,675 drives, 431 drivers, 1,380 hours, 85,919 km). On 776 evaluation drives from 94 unseen drivers, we compare six re-implemented attacks and benchmark baselines under explicit information-access protocols, paired comparisons, and metrics incorporating failures. Experiments show that combining steering signals with road-network constraints yields the largest gain: With a known start and heading, adding steering to speed raises the online map filter's five-minute route recovery from 56% to 87%, with a median average displacement error of 43 m versus 921 m for map-free dead reckoning. Offline beam search recovers 88% of test routes with the heading and 81% without it. Because methods fail on different windows, we also evaluate an LLM harness that selects among candidate routes on 659 five-minute windows; its best configuration recovers 79% of routes on test and 83% on few-shot, outperforming the best baseline on test and matching it on few-shot. Data and code at huggingface.co/datasets/HenryYHW/CANTraj and github.com/WangYuHang-cmd/GPS--CAN.
tldr: The paper releases CANTraj, a naturalistic driving dataset pairing decoded CAN-bus events with time-aligned GNSS trajectories, and benchmarks six trajectory-recovery attacks plus an LLM-based route-selection harness.
motivation: Removing GPS coordinates from shared driving logs is claimed to protect privacy, but speed, steering, and driving-event signals in CAN data may still leak location information; prior route-inference attacks used inconsistent assumptions and small datasets, so comparability and real-world effectiveness were unclear.
method: The authors build a large naturalistic dataset (3,940 drives, 454 drivers) with decoded CAN events and GNSS ground truth, define an evaluation benchmark and explicit information-access protocols, re-implement six attacks, and test road-network-constrained map filtering, beam search, dead reckoning, and an LLM harness that selects among candidate routes.
result: Adding steering to speed raises five-minute route recovery of an online map filter from 56% to 87% (median average displacement error 43 m vs 921 m for map-free dead reckoning); offline beam search recovers 88% of routes with known heading and 81% without, while the best LLM configuration recovers 79% on test and 83% on few-shot.
conclusion: CAN signals carry substantial location information, so omitting GPS is insufficient for privacy; standardized benchmarks and failure-aware metrics are needed to compare trajectory-recovery attacks.

title: VellSSLH: Sound Type-Guided Selective Speculative Load Hardening For Llvm Ir
authors: Swarn Priya
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18463v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Constant-time cryptographic programs written in C can still leak secrets during speculative execution. Mispredicted branches may allow instructions to access secret data and expose it through observable behavior. Speculative load hardening (SLH) addresses these leaks, but protecting values unnecessarily can introduce significant runtime overhead. We present VellSSLH, which selectively inserts speculative load hardening at LLVM IR. Programmers specify Public and Secret inputs in annotated C programs, and our analysis infers which values may become secret during speculation. The transformation then inserts misspeculation-flag operations and protections only where needed. VellSCT, our extracted checker, validates the resulting LLVM IR. We formalize speculative constant-time (SCT) security by extending Vellvm's LLVM semantics with speculative execution, attacker directives, and leakage observations. Our security type system reasons about SSA joins, symbolic values, poison, pointer provenance, and observable faults, and supports declared declassifications and trusted external services. In Rocq, we prove that programs accepted by the checker satisfy SCT, and that a reference hardening transformation preserves architectural behavior. Evaluated optimized variants are rechecked for SCT but are not covered by this preservation proof. Our mechanized guarantees apply at LLVM IR; security of the generated binary additionally depends on backend and hardware assumptions. We evaluate VellSSLH on 24 cryptographic entries on a bare-metal Intel processor. VellSSLH achieves 4.03% lower geometric-mean runtime than LLVM SLH, with 13 comparisons favoring VellSSLH, eight favoring LLVM SLH, and three inconclusive. For X25519, VellSSLH improves runtime by 22.69% over LLVM SLH with only 1.86% overhead over unprotected code. Compared with Ultimate SLH, VellSSLH achieves 19.65% lower runtime.
tldr: VellSSLH is a compiler-level, type-guided selective speculative load hardening pass for LLVM IR that reduces the overhead of constant-time cryptographic code.
motivation: Constant-time C cryptographic programs can still leak secrets through speculative execution, but existing speculative load hardening (SLH) instruments values unnecessarily, incurring large runtime costs.
method: Programmers annotate Public/Secret inputs; a security type system over an extended Vellvm semantics (with speculation, attacker directives, and leakage observations) infers which values may become secret, and a transformation inserts misspeculation-flag operations and protections only where needed, with a Rocq-verified checker (VellSCT) and preservation proof for a reference hardening transformation.
result: On 24 cryptographic benchmarks on a bare-metal Intel processor, VellSSLH achieves 4.03% lower geometric-mean runtime than LLVM SLH, and for X25519 a 22.69% speedup over LLVM SLH with only 1.86% overhead over unprotected code; against Ultimate SLH it is 19.65% faster.
conclusion: Selective, type-guided speculative hardening can substantially cut overhead while maintaining mechanized speculative constant-time guarantees at the LLVM IR level, though binary-level security still depends on backend and hardware assumptions.

title: PF-Exec: Large-Scale Uav Relay Load Balancing With An Anchored Potential Direction Decider And A Per-Dimension Gain-Learning Executor
authors: Liheng Zeng, Hanzhang Jia, Yiran Li, Yi Gao, Bo Ma
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17492v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Relay load balancing in large-scale UAV networks requires joint decisions on association, bandwidth, power and hovering position, while the dimension grows with the number of UAVs and each UAV sees only its local state. This paper splits the decision into two layers. An anchored potential direction decider emits a closed-form target at every instant and returns its direction only. A gain-learning executor maps a local observation into a positive gain per dimension, composes gain and target, and clips the action against the physical single-step bound; the two layers form PF-Exec. The unit gain is the default start, so the executor reduces to the pure potential policy before training. The load is first-order homogeneous in bandwidth, making the bandwidth target closed form, and the position target is the demand-weighted centroid of the served users. The system uses a two-hop access and millimetre-wave backhaul link with soft association, a 3GPP UMa-AV channel with two shadowing layers, an OU-type social-force crowd and a quadrotor physical layer. Evaluation spans all fleet sizes, two crowd scenarios, independent seeds, the published baselines in their own settings and a degraded-information line. In the highest-pressure burst setting the fixed-step comparison breaks down on part of the seeds, losing fairness and mean load at once, while PF-Exec holds fairness near one. Among the ten comparison methods only the greedy heuristic survives that setting; its load variance stays far higher. Under stale global state and position noise the fairness index stays high at both largest-scale scenarios. Flight energy is nearly identical between the learned and the fixed-step executor, and three constants are fixed once across all settings. The convergence properties of both layers, from the truncated gain iteration to the perturbed tracking bound, are proved in the companion analysis.
tldr: PF-Exec is a two-layer learning-based method for relay load balancing in large-scale UAV networks, combining a closed-form potential-direction decider with a per-dimension gain-learning executor.
motivation: Large-scale UAV relay networks require joint optimization of association, bandwidth, power, and hovering position under local information constraints, which is difficult for standard fixed-step or centralized approaches.
method: The approach separates decision-making into an anchored potential direction decider that outputs a target direction and a gain-learning executor that learns positive per-dimension gains from local observations, with action clipping against physical single-step bounds.
result: PF-Exec maintains fairness near one under high-pressure burst settings and stale/noisy global information, outperforming most baselines while keeping flight energy comparable to a fixed-step executor.
conclusion: The method provides a scalable load-balancing solution for UAV relay networks, with convergence and tracking guarantees deferred to a companion analysis.

title: A Realizability-Based Kinetic-Fluid Domain Decomposition Method For Single-Temperature Gas Mixtures
authors: Domenico Caparello, Lorenzo Pareschi, Thomas Rey
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces a domain-adaptive numerical method for multi-species kinetic models that relax toward a single-temperature and single-velocity hydrodynamic limit. To this end, we derive moment realizability matrices for this regime. In this way the ideas of Levermore, Morokoff, and Nadiga are extended to non-equilibrium mixtures in which inter-species and intra-species collisions occur at comparable rates, so that all species relax to a common velocity and a common temperature. The realizability conditions are used as an indicator to divide the computational domain, at each time step, into macroscopic and kinetic regions. In the kinetic regions, where the continuum description fails (e.g., across strong shocks, non-equilibrium interfaces, or kinetic boundary layers), the method solves the multi-species kinetic equations. Close to local thermodynamic equilibrium, the Euler equations of the mixture are solved instead. Confining the kinetic computations to the non-equilibrium regions reduces the simulation time, while the results remain close to those of the full kinetic solver. The method is discretized on Cartesian grids with high-order schemes in space and time. The kinetic equations are integrated with an Asymptotic-Preserving Implicit-Explicit (IMEX) scheme, so that a consistent discretization of the single-velocity, single-temperature Euler system of the mixture is recovered when the Knudsen number goes to zero. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first realizability-based adaptive spatial domain decomposition method for gas mixtures in this single-velocity, single-temperature setting.
tldr: The paper introduces a realizability-based domain decomposition method for multi-species kinetic equations that relax to a single-temperature, single-velocity Euler hydrodynamic limit.
motivation: Multi-species kinetic simulations are computationally expensive, especially when much of the domain is near local thermodynamic equilibrium and a macroscopic fluid description suffices.
method: The authors derive moment realizability matrices for single-temperature gas mixtures and use them as an indicator to split the domain into kinetic and macroscopic regions, solving kinetic equations with an asymptotic-preserving IMEX scheme in non-equilibrium regions and Euler equations elsewhere.
result: The adaptive method reduces simulation time while producing results close to full kinetic solvers, with high-order spatial and temporal discretization on Cartesian grids.
conclusion: This is presented as the first realizability-based adaptive spatial domain decomposition method for gas mixtures in the single-velocity, single-temperature regime.

title: I2c-grpo: Insight Importance Checklist For Reinforcement Learning In A Multi-Agent DDoS Alert Triage Workflow
authors: Eyal Zloof, Shaun Shuster, Aviram Zilberman, Chen Frydman, Inderjeet Singh, Andr\'es Murilo, Asaf Shabtai, Yuval Elovici, Rami Puzis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17534v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for investigative tasks over incomplete evidence, such as cybersecurity alert triage, but reinforcement learning (RL) for such tasks is difficult: intermediate steps have no verifiable labels, rollouts are costly, and outcome rewards are sparse. We propose Insight Importance Checklist (I2C)-GRPO, a checklist reward for intermediate investigation steps. For each decision point, a panel of expert LLMs proposes investigative actions, their atomic forensic insights are extracted, and a separate three-model ranker panel orders the insights by importance. A reward model checks which ranked insights a candidate action targets and returns their consensus-weighted coverage. Because actions are scored without being executed, the reward is a proxy for expected investigative value, and training reduces to a one-step contextual bandit over fixed investigation prefixes. From a soft-computing perspective, the reward is an additive fuzzy measure whose rank-exponent weights act as an ordered weighted averaging (OWA)-type operator; one exponent sets its orness, i.e., how strongly the reward concentrates on the top of the judges' consensus. We train an open-weight Qwen3-4B Triage Agent within a fixed multi-agent Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) alert-triage workflow on DARPA 2000 LLDOS 1.0 and test it on an independent CSE-CIC-IDS2018 DDoS trace. Across three training seeds, the agent reaches a mean F1-score of 0.869, 5.9 and 9.7 points above uniform insight weights and DIVA, and a false-positive rate of 4.9% versus 16.4% for GPT-5-mini. Within the weighting family, false positives fall only at the highest-orness weighting evaluated. All claims are limited to DDoS alert triage; the code, task contexts, and ranked insight dataset will be released.
tldr: The paper introduces I2C-GRPO, a checklist-based reward method for training LLM agents on multi-agent DDoS alert triage tasks with sparse and unverifiable intermediate rewards.
motivation: Reinforcement learning for LLM agents in cybersecurity investigation is challenging because intermediate steps lack verifiable labels, rollouts are costly, and outcome rewards are sparse.
method: A panel of expert LLMs proposes investigative actions and extracts atomic forensic insights, which are ranked by importance; a reward model scores candidate actions by consensus-weighted coverage of ranked insights, trained as a one-step contextual bandit over fixed prefixes.
result: On DARPA 2000 LLDOS 1.0 and CSE-CIC-IDS2018 DDoS traces, a Qwen3-4B triage agent reaches mean F1 0.869, outperforming uniform insight weights and DIVA by 5.9 and 9.7 points, with false-positive rate 4.9% versus 16.4% for GPT-5-mini.
conclusion: I2C-GRPO provides an effective proxy reward for intermediate investigative steps in LLM-based DDoS alert triage, with gains limited to that domain and released code, task contexts, and ranked insight dataset.

title: Evidence-Carrying Transport Across Effects
authors: F\'{e}lix Castro, Liron Cohen, Ariel Grunfeld, \'{e}tienne Miquey
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A program logic proved sound against one effectful semantics need not remain sound when the effect is re-implemented, yet the semantic relationship between reasoning before and after a change of effect is usually left implicit and re-established by hand. This paper provides a uniform, proof-relevant account of it. Working in realizability, where a notion of computation determines a model whose entailments carry explicit program evidence, we introduce simulations between effectful realizability cores, generalizing Longley's applicative morphisms to computation over an arbitrary strong monad. A single simulation transports the source logic along a ladder: it induces a morphism of the associated evidenced frames and, functorially, of the induced triposes. These passages are [MATH]-fully-faithful, so the three levels agree and a change of effect carries the entire higher-order program logic together with the evidence witnessing each derivation. A computationally dense simulation moreover computes a modality on the source logic, a nucleus through which the transport factors and which marks exactly the reasoning stable under the change, read off from the translation rather than postulated. This recovers known examples such as the double-negation modality of classical realizability, and examples such as sheafification arise from a modal refinement of the construction. Overall, the framework makes a change of effect a first-class object, one that can be composed, factored through its modality, and shown in cases not to exist, opening a path to transporting verified reasoning across effects.
tldr: The paper develops a proof-relevant framework for transporting program logics and evidence across changes of computational effects using simulations between effectful realizability cores.
motivation: A program logic proved sound for one effectful semantics may not remain sound when the effect is reimplemented, and the relationship between reasoning before and after such a change is typically implicit and re-established manually.
method: The authors work in realizability and introduce simulations between effectful realizability cores, generalizing Longley's applicative morphisms to computation over an arbitrary strong monad; these simulations induce morphisms of evidenced frames and triposes.
result: A single simulation transports the higher-order program logic together with its evidence, and a computationally dense simulation yields a modality/nucleus that characterizes exactly the reasoning stable under the change of effect.
conclusion: The framework makes a change of effect a first-class object that can be composed, factored through its modality, or shown not to exist, enabling transport of verified reasoning across effects.

title: Go Under Chinese Rules With A Succinct Game History Is Complete For Exponential Space
authors: Felix Czerner Markus Bl\"aser
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The complexity of games is a central topic in combinatorics, algorithms, and computational complexity theory. It asks how difficult it is to determine the winner of a combinatorial game under optimal play. Many games, such as Hex or Othello, are PSPACE-complete: the game tree has polynomial depth, so the game can be decided in PSPACE. However, some games allow exponentially long plays, for instance Chess (without a generalized 50-move rule) or Go under Japanese rules; these are complete for exponential time. To prevent infinite games, some games employ a no-repetition rule (super-ko rule), for instance Go under Chinese rules. Robson (1984) proved that Chess and Checkers with a no-repetition rule are even harder: deciding whether the first player has a winning strategy is EXPSPACE-complete. Since then, it has been an open problem whether Go with a no-repetition rule is EXPSPACE-complete, too. The complexity of a game under a no-repetition rule is typically interpreted as follows: given a board position, decide whether the first player has a winning strategy such that no repetition occurs from that position on. We introduce the concept of a succinct game history: a Boolean circuit that, given a board position, outputs 1 if the position is in the game history and 0 otherwise. It serves as a "judge" that tells the players whether a move is illegal because it creates a repetition. We prove that deciding whether Black has a winning strategy in Go with a no-repetition rule is EXPSPACE-complete when the game history is given succinctly. Moreover, the starting position in our hardness proof is reachable by legal gameplay, which has not always been the case in prior proofs.
tldr: The paper proves that deciding the winner in Go under Chinese rules with a succinctly encoded no-repetition game history is EXPSPACE-complete.
motivation: The complexity of Go with a no-repetition rule had remained open since Robson's EXPSPACE-completeness results for Chess and Checkers with no-repetition rules.
method: The authors introduce succinct game histories represented by Boolean circuits that act as judges for repetition legality, and use them to construct a reduction establishing EXPSPACE-hardness.
result: They show that deciding whether Black has a winning strategy in Go with a no-repetition rule is EXPSPACE-complete when the game history is given succinctly, with a starting position reachable by legal gameplay.
conclusion: The work resolves a long-standing open problem in combinatorial game complexity and strengthens prior hardness proofs by ensuring the initial position is legally reachable.

title: Relabeling Symmetry And Conservation Laws In Hydrostatic And Nonhydrostatic Upper-ocean Models
authors: F. J. Beron-Vera
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17597v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We explicitly identify conserved integrals of hydrostatic and nonhydrostatic reduced-gravity upper-ocean models, both vertically unrestricted and columnar, with Noether quantities associated with particle relabeling. The columnar velocity reduction preserves the Lie-algebra structure, providing a common Euler--Poincar\'e framework for both families.
