title: Lean-PEP: Performance-Estimation Certificates To Formally Verified Algorithmic Bounds
authors: Andersen Ang Xinyuan Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17618v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Performance-estimation certificates describe worst-case bounds for optimization algorithms. Turning a certificate into a formal theorem requires exact verification of its algebra and a connection between its coordinates, constraints and objective and the intended function-level problem. Lean-PEP provides a reusable interface for this task. It checks a submitted source and exact certificate against a supported canonical finite model, and a parameterized analytic theorem transfers the resulting finite bound to every admissible algorithm trajectory. Generated computation proofs discharge the obligations that depend on each certificate. An additional capture entry checks the numerical record and reconstruction policy. The implemented two-step proximal-gradient consumer verifies a new input with normalized bound 62500/499999, and a fixed eight-configuration batch yields seven distinct payloads with accepted certificates and executed Lean proofs. PG/GD cases and one-step attainment witnesses establish the corresponding algorithmic conclusions, and a fresh installation reproduces consumption of the supplied input. These results show how new certificate data can reuse a proved analytic interface to obtain function-level bounds within the supported models.
tldr: Lean-PEP is a Lean-based framework that turns performance-estimation certificates for optimization algorithms into formally verified, function-level convergence bounds.
motivation: Performance-estimation certificates give worst-case bounds for optimization algorithms, but making them rigorous requires exact algebraic verification and a bridge from certificate coordinates to the intended function-level problem.
method: The authors build a reusable Lean interface that checks a submitted source and exact certificate against a canonical finite model, then applies a parameterized analytic theorem to transfer the finite bound to all admissible algorithm trajectories, with generated computation proofs discharging per-certificate obligations.
result: A two-step proximal-gradient consumer is verified with normalized bound 62500/499999, and a fixed eight-configuration batch produces seven distinct accepted certificate payloads with executed Lean proofs, reproducible on a fresh installation.
conclusion: New certificate data can reuse a proved analytic interface to obtain function-level algorithmic bounds within the supported models, demonstrating a practical route to formally verified optimization guarantees.

title: iGRAIL: Blockchain-Based Generative Federated Learning For Trustworthy Healthcare Intelligence
authors: Debashis Das, Sourav Banerjee, Saraju P. Mohanty
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17703v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Healthcare organizations collect huge amounts of patient data from clinical records, medical tests, monitoring systems, and healthcare services. Such data can underpin intelligent healthcare analytics but remains distributed across institutions and cannot be shared directly due to privacy, security, and trust concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative learning without sharing raw patient records, but the exchanged model information remains vulnerable to privacy leakage, tampering, replay, and unauthorized access. In this paper, we propose iGRAIL, a blockchain-enabled generative FL framework for trustworthy healthcare intelligence. iGRAIL combines local generative learning for data augmentation with differential privacy to protect sensitive information during local training. Model communication is secured using cryptographic mechanisms, and blockchain-based verification and smart-contract access control ensure that only authorized, authentic, fresh, and integrity-preserving updates are accepted for federated aggregation. The framework is evaluated on four healthcare datasets and compared with the conventional FL and blockchain-based FL (BC-FL) under predictive, privacy, non-IID, scalability, malicious-update, security-verification, and runtime settings. For the two large diabetes datasets, iGRAIL improves accuracy by about 5.4-5.6%, the F1-score by 14.6-16.9%, and MCC by 16.0-18.1% over the best FL or BC-FL baseline. Increasing the strength of differential privacy reduces the privacy-loss parameter [MATH] by about 72.5% for the cancer dataset and 87.5% for the diabetes dataset, with only a limited loss in prediction performance. These results indicate that iGRAIL supports secure and scalable federated computing while preserving privacy, model integrity, and controlled participation, at the cost of additional computational overhead.
tldr: iGRAIL is a blockchain-enabled generative federated learning framework that combines local generative data augmentation, differential privacy, and smart-contract-based access control to enable privacy-preserving collaborative healthcare analytics.
motivation: Healthcare data is distributed across institutions and cannot be shared directly due to privacy, security, and trust concerns, while conventional federated learning still exposes exchanged model updates to leakage, tampering, replay, and unauthorized access.
method: The framework couples local generative learning for data augmentation with differential privacy during local training, secures model communication with cryptographic mechanisms, and uses blockchain verification plus smart-contract access control to admit only authentic, fresh, integrity-preserving updates into federated aggregation.
result: Across four healthcare datasets, iGRAIL improves accuracy by roughly 5.4-5.6%, F1-score by 14.6-16.9%, and MCC by 16.0-18.1% over FL and BC-FL baselines on two diabetes datasets, while stronger differential privacy cuts the privacy-loss parameter by about 72.5% (cancer) and 87.5% (diabetes) with limited predictive degradation.
conclusion: The authors conclude that iGRAIL supports secure, scalable federated computing that preserves privacy, model integrity, and controlled participation, at the cost of additional computational overhead.

title: Evaluating The Robustness Of Prnu Source-Camera Attribution To The Fingerprint-Copy Attack: An Open Toolkit With Triangle-Test Detection
authors: Zeno J. M. H. Geradts
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photo-Response Non-Uniformity (PRNU) is the de facto standard trace for sensor-level source-camera attribution, and a high Peak-to-Correlation-Energy (PCE) between a questioned image and a camera reference fingerprint is routinely treated as strong evidence of common origin. The fingerprint-copy attack of Goljan, Fridrich and Chen (2011) shows that this signal can be forged: an adversary who estimates a target camera's fingerprint from that camera's publicly available images can inject a scaled copy of it into an unrelated photograph, producing a forgery that clears a PCE decision threshold despite never having been taken by the target device. We present prnucf, an open, auditable toolkit that pairs a reference implementation of the (additive) fingerprint-copy attack with the triangle-test detector and a cohort-calibrated decision procedure, so that practitioners can quantify how fragile a PRNU attribution is against this attack on their own pipelines. On a controlled multi-camera Monte-Carlo benchmark the attack reaches an arbitrary target PCE at a mean PSNR of 59.2 dB (visually lossless), yet the triangle test separates forgeries from innocent images with an area under the ROC curve of 0.999, detecting every forgery at a cohort-calibrated 5% false-positive operating point. We discuss why a fixed significance cut-off is not safe in casework, the limitations of synthetic validation, and the open problem of extending explainable detection to the modern, GAN-based generation of fingerprint-transfer attacks. The toolkit is released under the MIT license with an explicit dual-use statement.
tldr: An open-source toolkit (prnucf) that implements the PRNU fingerprint-copy forgery attack alongside a triangle-test detector to quantify how fragile photo-response non-uniformity source-camera attribution is.
motivation: PRNU correlation (PCE) is routinely treated as strong forensic evidence, but the 2011 fingerprint-copy attack shows the signal can be forged, so practitioners need auditable tools to assess attribution robustness in their own pipelines.
method: The authors pair a reference implementation of the additive fingerprint-copy attack with the triangle-test detector and a cohort-calibrated decision procedure, then evaluate on a controlled multi-camera Monte-Carlo benchmark and discuss the pitfalls of fixed significance cut-offs in casework.
result: The attack reaches arbitrary target PCE values at 59.2 dB mean PSNR (visually lossless), while the triangle test separates forgeries from innocent images with AUC 0.999, detecting every forgery at a 5% false-positive operating point.
conclusion: The toolkit enables practical robustness auditing of PRNU attribution and highlights open problems such as extending explainable detection to GAN-based fingerprint-transfer attacks; it does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Disenfranchisement In Spatial Voting Games
authors: Joel Nishimura Vincent Lageschulte
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18468v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The questions of voting rights, group membership, and the boundaries of acceptable discourse all involve a recursive, self-stability issue, wherein the voters, group members, and acceptable commentators are often the ultimate arbiters of their own rules for inclusion and exclusion. In order to understand how ideological or issue diversity may impact the stability of such inclusion and exclusion, we introduce franchise elections, where voting members of a group vote to change the electorate. In particular, when agents are positioned inside an ideological or issue space, a social choice function that aggregates agent viewpoints induces a preference for agents over group composition, where agents prefer groups that improve the social choice function outcome for them. We demonstrate that when ideological space is two-dimensional, these franchise elections can generate complex behavior and that this complexity exists for any social choice function. Using the Yolk social choice function from voting theory, we illustrate that franchise elections can predict that agents attempting to introduce a new ideological axis perpendicular to an existing left-right spectrum risk disenfranchisement unless they ally with either side of the spectrum, and that franchise elections can cycle with any period.
tldr: The paper introduces franchise elections in spatial voting games to study how groups can recursively alter their own electorate and how ideological diversity affects inclusion/exclusion stability.
motivation: Voting rights, group membership, and acceptable discourse involve recursive self-stability problems where voters are often the arbiters of their own inclusion rules.
method: Agents are placed in an ideological issue space, and a social choice function induces preferences over group composition; the authors analyze franchise elections using spatial voting models and illustrate with the Yolk social choice function.
result: In two-dimensional ideological space, franchise elections can generate complex behavior for any social choice function, including cycling with any period and risks of disenfranchisement for agents introducing a perpendicular ideological axis unless they ally with an existing side.
conclusion: Franchise elections provide a formal way to understand instability in self-determined group boundaries and highlight how spatial ideology and coalition dynamics can lead to complex inclusion/exclusion outcomes.

title: Ozone Groups And Fixed Rings Of Double Ore Extensions
authors: Andr\'es Rubiano
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We determine centers of two families of four-dimensional double Ore extensions without torsion assumptions, restricting to [MATH] in [MATH]. On the PI locus of [MATH], we classify the ozone groups and obtain normal commutative fixed rings of generic degree two over the center, including a nonmonogenic example. For an odd-torsion subfamily of [MATH], independent odd orders [MATH] yield ozone group [MATH], PI degree [MATH] and fixed-algebra PI degree [MATH], with unchanged center. A PI specialization of [MATH] has trivial ozone group.
tldr: This paper studies centers, ozone groups, and fixed rings of four-dimensional double Ore extensions in a purely algebraic setting.
motivation: The work aims to classify algebraic invariants of double Ore extensions without torsion assumptions and analyze PI-locus behavior.
method: The author determines centers of two families of double Ore extensions and classifies ozone groups and commutative fixed rings, including an odd-torsion subfamily.
result: The paper obtains normal commutative fixed rings of generic degree two, computes ozone groups and PI degrees for an odd-torsion subfamily, and identifies a PI specialization with trivial ozone group.
conclusion: The results advance the structure theory of double Ore extensions and their fixed rings, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Gusto: A Toolkit For Compatible Finite Element Dynamical Cores
authors: Jemma Shipton, Thomas M. Bendall, Colin J. Cotter, David M. Acreman, Timothy C. Andrews, Jack Betteridge, Alex Brown, Thomas H. Gibson, Nell Hartney, David A. Ham, Joshua Hope-Collins, Jeremy A. Pike, Connor J. Ward, Dan Witt
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17540v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gusto is a tool for rapid prototyping of new algorithms based on compatible finite element methods for discretising the fluid equations in the dynamical core of weather and climate models. In this context, the development of new algorithms typically follows a path that involves testing on a hierarchy of simpler equation sets sharing important features of the mathematical structure of the equation set solved by the dynamical core. Gusto provides compatible finite element spatial discretisations of the hierarchy of equation sets, along with a range of timestepping schemes. The code is modular so that different spatial and temporal discretisations can be combined and the same schemes can be applied to any of the equation sets. This facilitates fair comparison of the schemes and makes the extension of any algorithmic developments to the more complex equation sets more straightforward. In this paper we present Gusto to the community by describing the algorithms implemented in Gusto and showcasing their performance through a variety of test problems commonly used in numerical weather prediction.
tldr: Gusto is a software toolkit for rapid prototyping of compatible finite element discretisations and timestepping schemes for weather and climate dynamical cores.
motivation: Developing new numerical algorithms for weather and climate models requires testing on a hierarchy of simplified equation sets that share the mathematical structure of the full dynamical core, which is cumbersome without a unified, modular codebase.
method: The authors implement compatible finite element spatial discretisations for a hierarchy of equation sets together with multiple timestepping schemes in a modular framework, allowing arbitrary combinations of spatial and temporal discretisations to be applied to any equation set.
result: Gusto is demonstrated on a range of standard numerical weather prediction test problems, showing that algorithmic comparisons can be made fairly and that developments extend straightforwardly to more complex equation sets.
conclusion: Gusto provides a practical community tool that lowers the barrier to prototyping and benchmarking new dynamical core algorithms, though it lies entirely outside quantum information science.

title: Optimal Dividend Problem For A Threshold Dependent Surplus Process With Bounded Dividend Rate
authors: Zhongqin Gao, Panyu Wu, Xiaowen Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17656v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study optimal bounded-rate dividend payments for a diffusion surplus process whose drift and volatility change at a fixed surplus threshold. Optimal strategies admit an exhaustive classification into zero-threshold, positive single-threshold, two-boundary, and three-boundary configurations. The latter two configurations have separated dividend regions, which arise because the interface can reverse the monotonicity of the derivative of the value function with respect to the initial surplus. Multiband optimality requires an upward change in drift. Without prescribing a strategy in advance, we construct the unique bounded classical solution of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman transmission problem by varying the derivative at zero surplus and selecting the unique value for which the resulting solution agrees in both value and derivative with a bounded solution at a fixed sufficiently large surplus level. Verification identifies this solution with the value function and determines the optimal feedback strategy. For each configuration, we derive necessary and sufficient optimality conditions and characterize the switching boundaries through explicit formulas or equations in one unknown obtained by matching the value function and its derivative. The analysis also shows how changes in the drift and volatility of the upper regime affect the optimal value and dividend strategy. Numerical analysis illustrates how model parameters affect the optimal dividend regions.
tldr: This paper studies optimal bounded-rate dividend payments for a threshold-dependent diffusion surplus process and classifies optimal strategies into zero-, single-, two-, and three-boundary configurations.
motivation: The problem is motivated by optimal dividend control in insurance risk models where the surplus process has regime changes in drift and volatility at a fixed threshold.
method: The authors construct the unique bounded classical solution of a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman transmission problem by varying the derivative at zero surplus and matching a bounded solution at a large surplus level, followed by verification.
result: They provide necessary and sufficient optimality conditions for each configuration and characterize switching boundaries via explicit formulas or one-dimensional matching equations, with numerical illustrations of parameter effects.
conclusion: The analysis fully classifies optimal dividend strategies and shows how drift and volatility changes in the upper regime affect the optimal value and dividend regions.

title: Proximal Adam Algorithm For Nonsmooth Composite Optimization And Linear Convergence Under Proximal Pl Geometry
authors: Zhongyi Huang Xiaopeng Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17727v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze Adam-type methods for nonsmooth composite optimization problems [MATH], where [MATH] is smooth and [MATH] is convex, proper, and lower semicontinuous. The nonsmooth term is treated by a metric-weighted proximal map, while the smooth term is preconditioned by the Adam second-moment matrix. We prove a composite descent lemma whose constants depend explicitly on the spectral bounds of the adaptive metric and a residual--step equivalence that converts proximal step decay into subgradient stationarity. These yield an [MATH] bound on the minimum proximal stationarity residual for the deterministic proximal normalized gradient method without convexity of [MATH], and the same [MATH] rate for proximal Adam under quantitative momentum-alignment and residual-coherence conditions together with a metric-compatibility condition. By estimating the momentum error directly, the same [MATH] rate is also obtained without the momentum-alignment and residual-coherence assumptions. When the composite objective satisfies a proximal Polyak--{\L}ojasiewicz inequality, both algorithms and the relaxed proximal Adam scheme converge linearly with explicit contraction factors. Numerical experiments on a diagonal Lasso problem, two-dimensional image TV denoising, and two-dimensional elastic parameter identification illustrate the predicted stationarity and linear rates.
tldr: This paper analyzes proximal Adam-type methods for nonsmooth composite optimization and proves stationarity and linear convergence rates under proximal Polyak-Łojasiewicz conditions.
motivation: The work aims to provide convergence guarantees for adaptive gradient methods when applied to nonsmooth composite objectives, where the nonsmooth term is handled by a metric-weighted proximal map.
method: The authors derive a composite descent lemma, a residual-step equivalence, and momentum-error estimates for deterministic proximal normalized gradient and proximal Adam under metric-compatibility conditions.
result: They obtain O(1/√K) bounds on the minimum proximal stationarity residual and linear convergence with explicit contraction factors when a proximal Polyak-Łojasiewicz inequality holds, supported by numerical experiments on Lasso, TV denoising, and elastic parameter identification.
conclusion: The paper establishes convergence theory for proximal Adam in nonsmooth composite optimization, but it is purely a classical optimization contribution with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Minimaxity In Robust Nonparametric Regression: From Heavy-Tailed To Sub-Gaussian Assumptions
authors: Matey Neykov Yikun Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study nonparametric regression over star-shaped function classes under strong adversarial contamination. The clean (original) observations [MATH] are i.i.d. and satisfy [MATH], where [MATH], [MATH] is distributed as [MATH], and the noise is conditionally centered. An adversary may inspect the clean sample and replace at most [MATH] observation pairs. We assume that [MATH] is star-shaped with finite diameter [MATH]. Under a Bernstein-type moment condition on function increments and a bounded conditional second moment for the noise, we establish the matching lower and upper bounds of order [MATH], uniformly over admissible star-shaped function classes, therefore characterizing the minimax rate of estimation error, where \eta ^{*}:=\sup\left\{\eta >0: n\eta^2\leq\log \mathcal M _{}^{}(\eta,c)\right\}. Here [MATH] denotes the local metric entropy of [MATH] in [MATH], and [MATH] is a sufficiently large constant. Under a uniform relative sub-Gaussian condition on function increments and noise, the lower bound is adjusted to [MATH] while the upper bound improves to [MATH], yielding minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors.
tldr: This paper characterizes minimax optimal rates for nonparametric regression over star-shaped function classes under strong adversarial contamination, bridging heavy-tailed and sub-Gaussian regimes.
motivation: Robust estimation under adversarial contamination is important for reliable statistical learning, yet minimax rates over general star-shaped classes with only moment conditions were not fully characterized.
method: The authors establish matching lower and upper bounds using local metric entropy, a Bernstein-type moment condition on function increments, and bounded conditional second moments for the noise, refined to a uniform relative sub-Gaussian condition.
result: They derive minimax rates of order involving the local entropy-based quantity eta*, with a sub-Gaussian regime yielding improved upper bounds and an adjusted lower bound matching up to logarithmic factors.
conclusion: The work provides a sharp minimax theory for robust nonparametric regression over star-shaped classes, unifying heavy-tailed and sub-Gaussian settings.

title: Inferring Sensitive Events In Multi-Mode Cyber-Physical Systems Via Scheduling Side Channels
authors: Linh Thi Xuan Phan Yifan Cai
abstract: ArXiv:2611.17761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many cyber-physical systems (CPS) are multi-mode: they switch between operating modes with different tasksets and timing parameters in response to physical events or user activity. We show that these mode changes create a timing side channel: by altering the interference experienced by co-running tasks, they let an unprivileged co-resident observer infer sensitive events, such as a homeowner's arrival or a vehicle's route, from its own execution timing and, on multicore platforms, its core assignment. Existing schedule-based attacks and defenses miss this channel because they assume single-mode systems or target a specific, known victim task. We present STAMP, a lightweight attack that needs no knowledge of task parameters or scheduling policy, and works whether or not the system exposes its modes. On a ZoneMinder home-security deployment, STAMP identifies the modes with 94.7% accuracy on unseen hardware, using under 0.5% of one core. On ROS 2 AMCL with the Oxford RobotCar dataset, it identifies which of seven route segments a vehicle traversed with 86.0% accuracy on unseen platforms. A schedule-randomization defense lowers detection recall to 0.53, at which setting only 53.9% as many jobs finish on time. At higher noise ([MATH]), on-time job completion reduces to 14.4%, while introducing new leakage in 14.1% of the tasksets.
tldr: The paper demonstrates a timing side channel in multi-mode cyber-physical systems that allows an unprivileged observer to infer sensitive events from scheduling interference and core assignment.
motivation: Mode switches in multi-mode CPS alter task interference, creating a side channel missed by existing schedule-based attacks and defenses that assume single-mode systems or known victim tasks.
method: The authors present STAMP, a lightweight attack requiring no knowledge of task parameters or scheduling policy, and evaluate it on ZoneMinder home-security and ROS 2 AMCL robot-car deployments.
result: STAMP identifies modes with 94.7% accuracy on unseen hardware for ZoneMinder and 86.0% accuracy for seven route segments on unseen robot platforms, while a schedule-randomization defense reduces detection recall to 0.53 at significant timing cost.
conclusion: Multi-mode CPS scheduling creates a practical and previously overlooked side channel for inferring sensitive events, and naive randomization defenses can impose large performance penalties while introducing new leakage.

title: Beyond Bot Labels: Retrospective Consequence-Grounded Ranking Of Attributed Cache Harm In E-Commerce Logs
authors: Jisoo Kim, Youngwoo Seo, Seonghoon Jeong
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web caches reduce origin load and latency, but automated traffic can either warm them or evict objects shoppers reuse, lowering the cache hit ratio (CHR). Existing bot defenses generally infer automation from User-Agent (UA) strings or behavior rather than identify sessions that impose cross-session cache harm. We instead formulate the task as ranking sessions by eviction damage and propose consequence-grounded session ranking. A single chronological replay attributes each eviction-induced miss by a protected shopping session (a victim) to the session whose insertion last evicted the object. A behavioral model predicts the target from session behavior alone. Selected sessions bypass the cache but remain origin-served. In a controlled check of 539 non-victim sessions selected across harm levels, attribution order tracks victim-hit changes after removal (Spearman correlation 0.80). On a 12.7-million-request real trace, the top 1% of sessions carry 48.8% of attributed harm. Sessions without bot tags contribute 49.1% of this tier's harm. At the 20% request-volume target, the default conditional CHR difference reaches 93% of the UA baseline, which selects 47 times as many sessions. Six training seeds show little variation. This comparison conditions on the victims that remain, so we also report victim bypass. Local replay and retraining on a second store reproduce harm concentration and a top tier dominated by sessions without bot tags. These results establish attributed cross-session harm as an outcome-based target for retrospective cache audits and selective intervention design.
tldr: The paper proposes a retrospective, consequence-grounded ranking of web sessions by the cross-session cache eviction harm they cause in e-commerce logs, rather than classifying traffic as bots via User-Agent or behavior.
motivation: Automated traffic can evict cached objects that real shoppers reuse, lowering cache hit ratios, yet existing bot defenses infer automation from User-Agent strings or behavior instead of identifying sessions that actually cause cross-session cache damage.
method: A single chronological replay attributes each eviction-induced miss suffered by a protected shopping session to the session whose insertion last evicted the object; a behavioral model then predicts this target from session behavior alone, and selected sessions are made to bypass the cache while remaining origin-served.
result: Attribution order tracks victim-hit changes after removal (Spearman 0.80); on a 12.7-million-request trace the top 1% of sessions carry 48.8% of attributed harm, with sessions lacking bot tags contributing 49.1% of that tier's harm, and the approach selects far fewer sessions than a UA baseline at comparable request volume.
conclusion: Attributed cross-session cache harm is established as an outcome-based target for retrospective cache audits and selective intervention design, with results reproduced on a second store.
